item.title: The Doctor Is In: Could the City Have Settled Its Open Meetings Fight for Less?
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — Former City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez says the Alamogordo City Commission could have resolved its Open Meetings Act dispute months ago, without running up outside legal bills. She made the case on this week's "The Doctor Is In" segment with host Anthony Lucero on KALH Radio.

The segment centers on the citizen lawsuit over the hiring of City Manager Robert Stockwell. Chris Edwards and Concerned Citizens of Alamogordo filed the petition in the Twelfth Judicial District Court on June 2, 2026, after giving the City written notice of the alleged violations on May 5 (background). A judge has since refused to dismiss the case, and it is headed for a hearing on the merits (court ruling).

"Could this have been resolved months ago without spending taxpayer dollars on outside legal representation?" Hernandez asked.

Hernandez said that while she was still city manager, she recommended the Commission acknowledge a potential violation, disclose it voluntarily and take corrective action.

State law gives public bodies room to do that. Before a citizen can sue, the public body gets written notice and 15 days to act on the claim, and it can reconsider a challenged action at a properly noticed public meeting. Violations are also a misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of up to $500 per offense against an individual who is convicted.

"To me, voluntarily identifying and correcting a potential violation seemed far less costly than prolonged litigation," she said. She added that a voluntary fix could still be an option today, though it would not guarantee the lawsuit is dismissed.

Hernandez also addressed concerns raised at the time that she had a conflict of interest, since the dispute involved hiring her successor. Her recommendation, she said, was about protecting the City and taxpayers, not about who should hold the job.

Hernandez pointed to Commissioner Baxter Pattillo's description of doing the legwork on Stockwell's proposed contract and circulating documents to the Commission.

That, she said, raises the possibility of a rolling quorum: commissioners discussing public business through a series of private communications that together involve a quorum. She was careful to note that circulating documents is not necessarily a violation on its own, but said it raises questions worth examining.

Hernandez acknowledged the law is complicated. She said she has worked with it for seven years and still doesn't consider herself an expert. Still, she noted, the Commission received Open Meetings Act training in March and has had earlier training opportunities.

Hernandez pushed back on the idea that the City can simply recover its legal bills from the citizen if it prevails.

Under the Open Meetings Act, a winning public body is awarded court costs. It recovers attorney fees only if the court also finds the plaintiff sued without sufficient information and belief that good grounds supported the case (NMSA 10-15-3).

"A citizen seeking government transparency doesn't automatically become responsible for the City's attorney fees simply because they lose a lawsuit," she said. The longer the case runs, she added, the higher the bills climb.

"Government officials make mistakes. What matters is how they respond," Hernandez said. "Shouldn't protecting taxpayer dollars be just as important as winning a lawsuit?"

Hear the full conversation with Dr. Stephanie Hernandez and Anthony Lucero on "The Doctor Is In": Open Meetings Act — The Doctor Is In (YouTube). More programming at KALHRadio.org.

Disclosure: Chris Edwards, general manager of KALH Radio and Alamogordo Town News, is the petitioner in the lawsuit discussed here. The case continues with an expected motion ruling within a week and a court conference to discuss next steps.

item.title: 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News Alamogordo Honors Its Veterans on Veterans Day 2026
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — At 11 a.m. today, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, Alamogordo pauses to honor the men and women who have worn the uniform of the United States. In a city whose story has been tied to Holloman Air Force Base since 1942, Veterans Day is not an abstraction. It is the neighbor down the street, the retiree at the VFW, and the Airman who just came home from deployment.

The 108th anniversary of the World War I armistice falls midweek this year, so the community began its tribute early. Since Saturday, residents have lined 10th Street, filled the civic center and gathered at the airport to say thank you.

The observances opened Saturday, Nov. 7, with the annual Veterans Day Parade down 10th Street from Cuba Avenue to Maryland Avenue. The free parade was organized by Air Force Sergeants Association Chapter 1257 at Holloman (Town News).

Airmen of the 49th Wing marched alongside cadets of the Alamogordo High School Air Force Junior ROTC, and the Tiger marching band played the route (DVIDS). The Patriot Guard Riders staged that morning at Mountain View Church on Cuba Avenue to ride in the procession (Patriot Guard Riders).

The same day, the Alamogordo-White Sands Regional Airport held a free Open House and Veterans Appreciation Day with aircraft displays, food trucks and STEM activities. The city's Sounds of Freedom celebration filled Alameda Park (City of Alamogordo). On Tuesday night, AFSA Chapter 1257 hosted its 13th annual Veterans Appreciation Dinner at the Sgt. Willie Estrada Memorial Civic Center, free to local veterans and a guest.

Few New Mexico communities are as bound to the armed forces as Alamogordo. This past May, the city and Holloman received the 2025 Altus Community Support Award, their second win in three years (Holloman AFB). The honor recognizes the city's backing of the base and its families.

That bond keeps growing. In June the 49th Wing welcomed Col. Michael S. Mullin as commander, back for a second tour, as the wing moved to Air Combat Command (Town News). In July six 49th Wing Airmen, including two Security Forces leaders awarded the Bronze Star, were recognized for combat service in the Middle East (Air University). They are today's veterans in the making.

The city's older generations are honored, too. In April, Vietnam-era veterans Chris Hall and Lucio Vazquez came home from a Rio Grande Honor Flight trip to Washington, D.C., to a hero's welcome at Patron's Hall (Town News). Over Memorial Day weekend, more than 70 volunteers joined VFW Post 7686 at dawn to place flags on veterans' graves at Monte Vista Cemetery (Town News).

Groups like the U.S. Veterans MC Trinity Chapter, chartered here in 2018 on a mission of veterans helping veterans, carry that service forward all year (Town News).

The parade may be over, but there are simple ways to honor veterans today and beyond:

Veterans seeking benefits help can contact the New Mexico Department of Veterans' Services. Any veteran in crisis, or anyone worried about one, can call or text 988 and press 1 for the Veterans Crisis Line, available around the clock.

From the F-16s over the Tularosa Basin to the flags at Monte Vista Cemetery, Alamogordo lives alongside its service members every day. Today the city simply says it out loud.

To every veteran, active-duty member and military family in Alamogordo, Holloman, Tularosa and beyond: thank you for your service.

Note article by Chris Edwards, a journalist for 2nd Life Media affiliated sites. Mr Edwards is a strong advocate and supporter of the mission of the Honor Flights, the local VFW’s upgrades and its impact of support as a safe and diverse gathering place for our veterans, and supporting the mission of team Holloman and all of our area veterans.

item.title: Solar developer pitches three sites near Tularosa as neighbors press on flooding
item.description:
TULAROSA — A community solar developer told the Tularosa Planning and Zoning Commission on Tuesday that it hopes to build as many as three solar gardens in and around the village. Neighbors of one proposed site said they don't oppose solar power, but they urged officials to make sure the project doesn't worsen flooding that already damages their property.

SunShare Community Solar has filed special use permit applications for all three sites. The company says it built its first project in Colorado Springs in 2011. It now reports more than 220 megawatts developed, about 19,000 subscribers and operations in nine states.

"We're really excited to talk to you guys about three community solar gardens that we are proposing within the village of Tularosa," said Mike, an associate developer with the company. He presented with Keenan, SunShare's director of development for New Mexico.

Under New Mexico's Community Solar Act, passed in 2021, residents and small businesses can subscribe to a solar garden and receive credits on their PNM bills. SunShare said standard subscribers save 10%.

State rules require at least 30% of each project's output to go to low-income subscribers, at a discount of at least 20%. SunShare said its projects typically reserve 50% for low-income households and give them a 30% discount. New Mexico lets residents self-attest to low-income status.

Each project would be about 5 megawatts, enough for roughly 400 to 500 subscribers, according to the company. Signing up and opting out are free. The power would flow to PNM's Tularosa substation and be used locally.

Two sites sit off Moon Valley Road. The first, which SunShare calls the Cumbre project, lies next to an existing solar array built by a different company. A smaller parcel lies to its northeast. The third site is on the north side of town off Twelfth Street, with the railroad along its west edge.

SunShare said it bought one property and is leasing the other two. Leases run 20 years with optional five-year extensions, and each site needs about 30 acres. State rules require projects to be within a mile of a three-phase power line, which representatives said explains why the sites are close to homes.

The company described sites with an 8-foot, wildlife-friendly security fence, no lighting and no batteries. It said inverters run about 58 decibels and can't be heard beyond roughly 150 feet. SunShare said it would replant native vegetation, use no chemical herbicides and post a bond to cover eventual decommissioning.

Ann Farmer, who lives on Highway 54/70 just south of the proposed Moon Valley sites, told commissioners she has no complaint about solar panels themselves.

"I have no problem with the solar field itself because I've already got one across from me," Farmer said. "They're good neighbors. They're quiet. They don't block my view."

Her concern is drainage. Farmer said flooding from a nearby arroyo has gotten worse every year since a pellet plant built a bridge over it. The last storm washed out her driveway and reached the highway, partly closing the road into town, she said. Sediment has now built up higher than her land, and her family keeps having to raise the berm that protects her house.

"The good news is we don't have that much rain, but when it comes, it just about wipes me out," she said. She said a culvert near her neighbor's driveway stays clogged. When the state tried to clean it out, it left deep ruts, she said, and she got no reply after emailing photos to the highway department.

Rick Robbins, a 75-year-old retired military veteran who has lived on Moon Valley Road for 30 years, raised the same flooding concern. "It doesn't even have to rain here in Tularosa," he said. "If it rains on the mountain over there, it funnels down and comes across Moon Valley Road."

Robbins asked who would maintain the private road that construction crews would use. He also asked whether the panels would raise nearby temperatures, citing research he found that put the increase as high as 6 degrees. He also asked about snakes and wildlife, future expansion and property values.

SunShare representatives said they had already spoken with the landowner about the arroyo. They offered to add regular ditch cleanouts to the site's maintenance contract.

"There has never been, I guess, an actual agreement in place for someone to actually do that," one representative said. "I think this is an opportunity for us to actually address it." The company also noted that a stormwater management plan is required before it can get a building permit.

On roads, SunShare said it would sign a road use agreement, post a bond if the village requires one and repair any damage. On heat, representatives said studies of the "heat island effect" show solar arrays are not a significant concern. They said panels on single-axis trackers move through the day and trap far less heat than a parking lot.

The company said program rules allow only one project per parcel, which limits expansion. On property values, a representative said studies have found effects in both directions. SunShare said glare studies for all three sites found no impacts, and early environmental and cultural reviews came back favorable.

The commission took no vote Tuesday. For special use permits, the commission doesn't approve or deny. It sends findings of fact and conditional recommendations to the Village Council, which makes the decision. Commissioners said SunShare would get a copy of their findings.

Any approval would also depend on a state contest. The projects are competing in Phase 2 of the community solar program, a competitive request for proposals run by the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission. SunShare expects bidding to open in January or February. Awards are expected around June 2027.

"Maybe we are able to get one project or two projects, maybe all three, or maybe none," Keenan said. SunShare confirmed it cannot build without a state award. If it wins, construction would likely start in early 2028 and take about three months.

Commissioners raised possible conditions, including a list of native plants, a decommissioning bond that rises each year with inflation, and an access easement for the village in case it annexes the areas, which are now in its extraterritorial jurisdiction. SunShare said it was open to each.

Opportunity zone. The commission heard that Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham has nominated three Otero County census tracts for federal opportunity zone designation, one of them in Tularosa. The others cover Alamogordo's downtown and the corridor along the Charlie Lee Memorial Relief Route. The designation would give investors federal tax breaks for putting money into those areas from 2027 through 2036. Commissioners said federal approval is usually routine. They stressed that the village needs updated ordinances in place before investors arrive: vacant building registration, then development impact fees, then a historic preservation plan.

State permit dispute. The commission approved the permit for a completed re-roof at 710 First Street. The state Construction Industries Division had issued its own permit without going through the village. Village staff said they have written to all three CID offices and are following up by phone. The homeowner paid the village fee after the work was done.

Code enforcement. Commissioners can now issue a first-notice form for planning and zoning violations, created by the village's code enforcement officer, who will handle follow-up. Residents with complaints can call the police non-emergency line. The village's ordinances can be searched on its website.

New member. The commission welcomed new member Efren Gonzalez.

The meeting adjourned at 6:50 p.m.

item.title: Tigers Get Hometown Send-Off Before 5A Quarterfinal at Los Lunas
item.description:
Alamogordo N.M. - The Alamogordo Tigers are hitting the road for the biggest game of their season, and the town is being asked to give them a proper goodbye.

Alamogordo High School will hold a Tiger Football Playoff Send-Off at 2 p.m. Friday, Nov. 13, as the team departs for Saturday's Class 5A state quarterfinal against Los Lunas. Organizers are calling on students, families, alumni, local businesses and the wider community to turn out in black and gold.

Fans who can't make it to the school are encouraged to find a spot anywhere along the route to cheer the bus as it passes.

It's a Tigers-vs.-Tigers matchup. Fifth-seeded Alamogordo (7-4) earned the trip with a dominant 54-0 first-round shutout of district rival Chaparral last Friday, its fifth straight win. Over that five-game streak, Alamogordo's defense has given up just 47 points combined — fewer than it allowed in its season opener alone.

The offense was balanced against Chaparral. Junior quarterback Nathaniel Cereceres threw for 141 yards and two touchdowns and ran for 69 yards and another score on just seven carries. Junior receiver Tristan Bowman piled up 111 receiving yards, including a 76-yard catch, and scored both through the air and on the ground. Sophomore running back Qymani Patterson added 110 rushing yards and a touchdown, breaking off a 45-yard run.

Los Lunas (7-3) is in its first season in Class 5A after moving down from 6A and earned the No. 4 seed and a first-round bye under first-year head coach Stephen Johnston. The hosts are rolling too: they closed the regular season with a 50-0 rout of Highland, and quarterback Luke Cieremans threw four touchdown passes in that game. Los Lunas' defense has allowed only 33 points over its last seven games.

First-round results (Nov. 6–7)

Roswell, Piedra Vista, Artesia and Los Lunas had first-round byes as the top four seeds.

Quarterfinals (Nov. 13–14)

What's next: Semifinals are Nov. 20–21, and the Class 5A state championship is Nov. 28 at a finalist's home site. A win Saturday would put Alamogordo in the final four.

Other quarterfinals this weekend include Class 6A's No. 1 Cleveland hosting No. 9 Rio Rancho and No. 2 Volcano Vista hosting No. 7 Carlsbad; Class 4A's No. 1 Bloomfield hosting No. 8 Valencia; and Class 3A's No. 1 St. Michael's hosting No. 8 Pojoaque Valley. Six-man crowns its champion Nov. 14, eight-man on Nov. 21, and Classes 2A through 6A on Nov. 28.

All times Mountain. Records and statistics as reported by MaxPreps

item.title: In Memory of Juan Lucio Maes
item.description:
Juan Lucio Maes, of Tularosa, New Mexico, was born on January 19, 1948, and passed away on November 4, 2026. He proudly served in the United States Army and worked for 30 years in heating and cooling (HVAC) at Holloman Air Force Base.

Juan loved his family, music, and the Tularosa Wildcats. He coached little league baseball and soccer, and enjoyed hunting, camping, and fishing.

Juan deeply loved St. Francis de Paula Catholic Church and served there in many ways over the years. He participated as a Danzante, served as a Mayordomo, and was a member of the church committee. He helped organize and manage the annual fiestas, and each Christmas he organized the church’s Luminarias. Music, hot chocolate, and cookies brought the community together for the celebration. Juan’s generosity reached beyond the church as well helping anyone he could.

Juan is survived by his wife, Virginia Maes; his daughters, Helen Butler, Jessica Iverson, Brenda Maes; his sons-in-law, Christopher Butler, Robert Iverson, Calvin Lapaz. He also leaves eight grandchildren: Brendan Chavez, Kirsten Chavez, Logan Chavez, Raven Iverson, Abram Iverson, Job Maes, Theron La Paz, Genesis La Paz; three great grandchildren: Cayson Chavez, Easton Dorame, Cayden Dorame.

Pallbearers include Joe Provencio, Brendan Chavez, Logan Chavez, Robert Iverson, Abram Iverson, Calvin Lapaz, Job Maes, Theron La Paz.

Honorary pallbearers are Christopher Butler, Mark Chino, Anthony Fresques, Joyce Amaya, Janette Mata, Robert and Cynthia Maes, Gloria Sedillo, Rayburn Chico, Michael Coyazo, Benjamin Coyazo, Paul Rocha.

Services will take place at St. Francis de Paula Catholic Church in Tularosa, New Mexico on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Viewing will be held from 9:00 am to 10:00 am. Rosary will be recited at 10:00 am with Mass celebrated at 10:30 am. Juan will be laid to rest following services at Sacred Heart Cemetery in Tularosa.

Juan will be remembered for his service, faith, and the love and generosity he shared with his family and community.

item.title: In Memory of Norman Lane
item.description:
Norman Lane, 93, passed away peacefully on September 6, 2026, in Las Cruces, New Mexico. Born and raised in Cloudcroft, New Mexico, he later made Alamogordo his home for 68 years, eventually moving to Las Cruces, NM for health care.

Norman proudly served in the United States Navy during the Korean War. After his military service, he built a successful career as a businessman and land developer. His ventures included Lane Plumbing Co., inc. in 1962, Lane Good Housekeeping Store, Desert Hills Subdivision and many others. He gave generously of his time to the community through his involvement with the Noon Lions Club, the Masonic Lodge, and the Elks Lodge. He was also a longtime member of Grace United Methodist Church.

Norman is survived by his three children, Gary Lane (Wanda), Cheri Rabon (Randy), Debbie Moore; his seven grandchildren, Kayla Lane, Norman Jaret Lane (Katie), Kelsey Joy Lane, Kristy Alsleben (Matt), Chad Rabon (Paige), Cody Lane Craig (Nikki), Abe Moore (Juliett), Josh Moore (Christine); his 14 great grandchildren.

Family was at the heart of Norman's life. He was preceded in death by Joy, the love of his life. Together, they shared 69 wonderful years of marriage. He was also preceded in death by his parents, Les and Jennie Lane; his brothers, Rex "Buster" Lane, Gene Lane, Dutch Lane; his son-in-law, Doug Moore; his grandson, Eli Moore.

He leaves behind many special friends including his dear friend, Yvonne Brown, as well as countless lives he touched over the years.

Those who knew Norman will remember his strong work ethic, outgoing spirit, and love of life. He never met a stranger and enjoyed connecting with people wherever he went. He loved classic cars, traveling in his RV, watching sports, and spending many years making memories at Elephant Butte lake.

More than anything, Norman's greatest legacy was his family. He will be deeply missed and lovingly remembered by his children, grandchildren, great grandchildren, extended family, and many friends. He often told anyone who would listen how blessed he was and how grateful he felt to have lived 93 full and meaningful years.

A Celebration of Life will be held for Norman from 1:00 pm to 3:00 pm on Monday, November 23, 2026, at the Elks Lodge located at 2290 Hamilton Road in Alamogordo.

item.title: Alamogordo commission to weigh mayor's agenda role, closed-door complaint against city manager
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A  dispute in interpretation of Charter rules between Mayor Sharon McDonald and City Manager Robert Stockwell will play out on two fronts Tuesday, when the Alamogordo City Commission is set to decide how much control the mayor should have over meeting agendas and, behind closed doors, to consider a complaint involving Stockwell himself.

The regular meeting begins at 6:30 p.m. Nov. 17 in the Donald E. Carroll City Commission Chambers at City Hall, 1376 E. Ninth St.

Under an item titled "the Mayor's Role in the City Commission Agenda Process," Stockwell asks commissioners to clarify Rule 5(a) of Resolution 2018-08, which says only that the city clerk "shall consult with the City Manager and the Mayor" when preparing agendas.

According to Stockwell's written report in the agenda packet, McDonald recently emailed him and City Clerk Rachel Hughs saying she would take a more active role in building and finalizing agendas. She asked to receive a preliminary draft of each agenda with enough time to review it and meet with both officials before publication, and to be consulted on any later removal or significant change to agenda items. McDonald wrote that as presiding officer she has "a responsibility to be informed and adequately prepared," according to the report.

Stockwell argues the request adds steps that could delay getting the full packet to commissioners. Agenda items are due at noon the Tuesday before a meeting, he wrote, and building in time for the mayor's review would push that deadline back to the previous Friday. He noted that past mayors have occasionally sat in on agenda review meetings but were never given approval authority, and that the agenda is not formally adopted until the full commission votes on it at the start of each meeting.

Stockwell said he directed the clerk to follow the mayor's process for Tuesday's agenda, and his report lays out how that went: the first draft went to McDonald at 10:18 a.m. on a Tuesday, revisions followed at 3:04 p.m., and a reminder that staff were awaiting her approval went out at 4:45 p.m. McDonald gave her approval at 4:54 a.m. the next day, the report says. Stockwell added that an error was later found in identifying which department director the mayor wanted investigated, requiring yet another review before the agenda could be finalized.

"If the City Commission feels the request of the Mayor to enlarge her role in the agenda process is appropriate, then Rule 5(a) should be amended to clarify the process," Stockwell wrote.

Stockwell's report quotes from McDonald's email but does not include it. The full text of the email, addressed to Stockwell and City Clerk Rachel Hughs, reads:

City Manager Stockwell and City Clerk Hughs,

I am requesting that, effective immediately, I be included in the review of all City Commission agendas before they are finalized and published.

Under Resolution No. 2018-08, Rule 5(a), the City Clerk is required to consult with both the City Manager and the Mayor in preparing the agenda. Additionally, Rule 5(c) establishes that any Commission member may direct that matters within the Commission's jurisdiction be placed on the agenda.

As Mayor and presiding officer of the City Commission meetings I have a responsibility to be informed and adequately prepared for the business coming before the governing body. Meaningful participation in the agenda preparation process allows me to fulfill that responsibility, identify potential concerns, and ensure that matters requiring Commission consideration are appropriately presented.

While I recognize your respective administrative responsibilities, the agenda serves the governing body, and my involvement should occur before it is finalized.

Moving forward, I would like to receive a preliminary draft of each agenda with sufficient time to review it and meet with both of you before publication. I also expect to be consulted regarding any proposed removal or significant modification of agenda items following our review meeting.

This is not about interfering with administrative responsibilities. It is about ensuring that the Mayor's responsibilities and the procedures established by the City Commission are respected.

Please confirm that this review process will be incorporated into the preparation of future Commission agendas.

Thank you,

Mayor Sharon McDonald, City of Alamogordo

The email asks for review before publication and consultation on later changes. It does not claim authority to approve or veto agenda items. Stockwell's report contrasts the request with past mayors, who he says did their jobs "without asserting a role of approving drafts and the final submission" of the agenda.

Alamogordo has a commission-manager form of government: an elected commission sets policy and hires a manager to run the city day to day.

State law. Under NMSA 1978 Section 3-14-10, the mayor "shall preside at all meetings of the commission and perform other duties, consistent with his/her office, as imposed by the commission," and holds all the powers of a commissioner, including a vote on every question. Section 3-14-12 vests the city's governing powers in the commission as a body, and Sections 3-14-13 and 3-14-14 give daily administration to the manager. The law gives the mayor no administrative authority of her own, but leaves the commission free to assign her additional duties.

The city charter. Article VIII, Section 2 of the Alamogordo City Charter makes the mayor the presiding officer of commission meetings and the representative and voice of the city. 

The commission's own rules. Resolution 2018-08 sets the commission's meeting procedures. Rule 5(a) states that "the City Clerk shall consult with the City Manager and the Mayor" in preparing the agenda. The consultation is required, but the rule does not say when it must happen, what form it takes, or whether the mayor may approve, change or hold back items.

Past practice. Stockwell's report acknowledges that mayors have "on occasion" attended agenda review meetings with the manager and clerk, though he says those meetings never gave a mayor approval authority. McDonald has said pre-publication agenda meetings were routine under her three predecessors — Susie Galea, Richard Boss and Susan Payne — and that she is asking to restore that practice, not create a new one.

Former Mayor Susan Payne confirms McDonald’s assessment and disputes Stockwell’s assertion as an attempt to undermine over two decades of precedent. 

What commissioners must decide. The dispute comes down to what "consult" means. Read narrowly, as Stockwell reads it, the requirement is met by the existing manager-clerk review, with the agenda finalized when the full commission votes on it at the start of each meeting. Read broadly, it calls for the mayor's input while the agenda is still being drafted. Because state law lets the commission define the mayor's additional duties, commissioners can settle the question by leaving Rule 5(a) as written or by amending it to spell out the process — the option Stockwell's report raises.

Public comment is encouraged as the mayor is the only at large publicly elected official on the commission to represent the public at large.

Later in the meeting, the commission is scheduled to recess into executive session to discuss "the consideration and possible investigation of a complaint concerning the City Manager and the Community Development Director," an item placed on the agenda by McDonald. Shelley Dowhanik-Baron is the city's community development director.

The agenda lists a possible follow-up vote in open session to authorize an independent investigation of the complaint. The packet does not say who filed the complaint or what it alleges, and no supporting documents were included.

The city has no city attorney; the position is listed as vacant on the agenda. Resolutions in the packet are signed "approved as to form" by Stockwell.

Personnel issues in the Community Development Department have surfaced at recent meetings. During public comment on Oct. 27, former employee Justen Boyle told commissioners he believed his firing was retaliation for raising ADA-compliance and ordinance concerns with human resources, and that his grievance hearing was canceled with less than 24 hours' notice, according to draft minutes. At the same meeting, commissioners voted 7-0 after a closed session to have HR Director Michelle Osborne hire an independent reviewer for a separate personnel matter involving the city's senior project manager, with a deadline of Nov. 17. The agenda does not indicate whether either matter is connected to the new complaint.

Commissioners will also meet privately to discuss real property — specifically the sale of the Fairgrounds parking lot — with a possible vote afterward to authorize the sale. The packet does not name a buyer or a price.

On the consent agenda, Resolution 2026-38 would impose a six-month moratorium on new off-premise billboards, including new electronic billboards and conversions of existing billboards to electronic displays.

It would be the city's seventh such moratorium since 2018. The most recent one expired June 2, 2026. The resolution says billboards "can significantly detract" from the city's goals for aesthetics and image, and that the pause is meant to hold while the city updates its code of ordinances, including its sign rules. It covers elevated off-premise signs at least 4 feet off the ground with a face of 100 square feet or more.

Residents who want to speak during public comment must sign up with the city clerk; the standard time limit is three minutes. The full agenda packet is posted on the city's website. People needing disability accommodations should contact the City Clerk's Office at 575-439-4100 at least 48 hours in advance.

Sources: IPRA and City of Alamogordo Regular Meeting Agenda Book, Nov. 17, 2026, including agenda reports and draft minutes of the Oct. 27 and Nov. 3, 2026, meetings; Alamogordo City Charter; Resolution 2018-08; NMSA 1978, Sections 3-14-10 through 3-14-14.

item.title: Alamogordo Police Weekly Log: Shots-Fired Arrest, Four DWIs and a Busy Week for Animal Control, November 2–8, 2026
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Alamogordo Police Department's weekly activity log for November 2 through November 8, 2026, lists more than 60 arrests, citations, juvenile referrals and other incidents. They range from a shots-fired investigation to a string of animal-at-large citations. The log covers major activity only, not every call for service that week.

People named in police reports are presumed innocent until proven guilty in a court of law.

The full log is linked here:
https://coa-utilities.com/DocumentCenter/View/19245/November-2-to-November-8-2026-PDF

Most Serious Incidents

On Thursday, November 5, a shots-fired investigation led to an arrest. The charges were shooting at an occupied dwelling or from a motor vehicle, tampering with evidence, attempted tampering with evidence, and resisting an officer.

On Friday, a disturbance call ended in an arrest for robbery, aggravated assault on a peace officer, battery against a household member, and resisting arrest. On Saturday, another disturbance led to charges of aggravated burglary, battery and resisting an officer. A separate Saturday disturbance ended in an aggravated assault arrest.

On Wednesday, a welfare check led officers to serve a Magistrate Court warrant for aggravated assault against a household member with a deadly weapon.

On Thursday, a disturbance at Christus Health led to an arrest on two counts of battery on a healthcare worker, plus battery and disorderly conduct. The same day, officers looking into a stolen vehicle report found a suspect inside Walmart Supercenter. The suspect was charged with unlawful taking of a motor vehicle, criminal trespass and open container.

DWI and Traffic

Officers made four DWI arrests during the week:

At about 4:23 p.m. Monday, APD, the fire department and AMR crews responded to a crash at the 54/70 Bypass and 10th Street. Police say a grey Ford Ranger turned east without yielding and hit a northbound red Chevy truck. The truck's occupants were checked by AMR but declined to go to the hospital. The Ranger's driver was cited.

Drugs and Warrants

On Monday, APD helped the Narcotics Enforcement Unit arrest three people on Magistrate Court warrants for possession of a controlled substance. One of them also had a Village of Tularosa warrant. Another controlled-substance warrant was served Tuesday on someone already in jail at OCDC. On Thursday, a warrant arrest also brought a drug paraphernalia charge.

Warrant arrests made up a large share of the week. Most were for failure to appear or failure to pay. Others included:

Juveniles

Four juveniles appear in the log:

Disorderly Conduct, Trespass and Other Offenses

item.title: Alamogordo Man Held Without Bail on Child Sex Abuse Charge
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A 40-year-old Alamogordo man will stay in jail until trial on a charge that he sexually abused his 3-year-old daughter. A district judge found that no conditions of release would keep the community safe.

District Judge Daniel Bryant bound Amos Muncy over for trial on one count of criminal sexual contact of a child under 13, a second-degree felony. Muncy waived his right to a preliminary hearing. At the end of an Aug. 24 hearing, Bryant ordered him held without bail, and he filed his written findings on Sept. 11. If Muncy is convicted, he faces up to 15 years in prison.

In his dangerousness order, Bryant called the evidence against Muncy very strong. He gave significant weight to Muncy's criminal history. In 2012, Muncy pleaded guilty in Sierra County to raping and sexually abusing an 11-year-old girl. The judge noted that Muncy had gone through sex offender supervision and treatment and is now accused of a similar offense against a much younger child. "This is alarming," Bryant wrote.

The allegations

According to an arrest warrant affidavit filed by Otero County Sheriff's Office Sgt. Robert Welles, the girl's mother told investigators she woke up to find Muncy touching the child, who was asleep between them. The mother said she grabbed a machete and ordered him out of the house. She said Muncy claimed he had not realized where his hands were.

The mother did not call police. According to the affidavit, she told investigators she did not want to make things harder for her daughter, who is very attached to Muncy.

The investigation started Aug. 21, after the state Children, Youth and Families Department sent the sheriff's office a tip it had received three days earlier. Welles filed the warrant on Aug. 22, and Muncy was arrested on Aug. 24. He has been in custody since.

Prior conviction

In the 2012 case, the victim told a Truth or Consequences detective that Muncy, her stepfather, had repeatedly sexually abused her for about two years, starting when she was 11. Muncy received the mandatory minimum sentence of three years in prison, with the rest of his sentence suspended. He was discharged from probation in 2020.

Next steps

Prosecutors have asked the court to schedule a trial, which they expect to last three days. No hearing dates have been set.

The charges are allegations, and Muncy is presumed innocent unless proven guilty in court.

item.title: New Mexico’s 2026 “Blue Wave” Was Mostly a Republican Turnout Collapse
item.description:
2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News, New Mexico Conservative News Analysis- New Mexico Democrats expanded their margins in the 2026 midterm, but the raw vote counts and party-specific turnout rates tell a more precise story than the percentage margins that dominated much of the national coverage.

Overall turnout was roughly comparable to the last midterm — about 50 percent of registered voters cast ballots this year (roughly 729,000 ballots in unofficial returns out of approximately 1.47 million registered) versus 52.4 percent in 2022 (about 711,000–715,000 ballots out of 1.36 million registered).

The difference was who showed up — and, just as important, who didn't.

In 2022, Republicans turned out at a higher rate than Democrats. Secretary of State figures reported by Source NM put 2022 turnout at roughly 61 percent of registered Republicans versus 57 percent of registered Democrats. Independents lagged far behind.

In 2026 the rates reversed: Democrats reached approximately 61–62 percent turnout while Republicans fell to about 53 percent and independents remained near 32 percent.

The state's registered voter pool had grown by roughly 100,000 people, which is why total ballots cast were slightly higher even as the percentage declined.

The partisan composition of the electorate, however, shifted.

In the 2022 gubernatorial race, Michelle Lujan Grisham (D) defeated Mark Ronchetti (R) with about 370,000 votes (52 percent) to roughly 325,000 (45.6 percent) — a margin of about 6 points.

In 2026, Deb Haaland (D) received approximately 416,000 votes (57.4 percent) while Republican Gregg Hull received about 309,000 (42.6 percent), a margin of nearly 15 points — far wider than the 6- to 7-point gap fall polling had shown.

Democratic raw totals rose modestly from the previous midterm; Republican raw totals declined. The margin more than doubled.

Similar patterns appeared in other statewide contests, including the U.S. Senate race, where Ben Ray Luján faced no Republican on the primary ballot at all.

Early and absentee voting amplified the difference.

Democrats banked a larger share of their registrants before Election Day in 2026 than they had in 2022 — roughly 238,000 registered Democrats voted early or absentee, compared with about 143,000 Republicans.

Republicans continued their traditional Election Day lean (about 94,000 voted on Nov. 3), but they began from a deficit of more than 100,000 ballots that Election Day could not close.

The clearest illustration is New Mexico's 2nd Congressional District.

Gabe Vasquez first won the seat in 2022 by roughly 1,350 votes (50.3 percent to 49.6 percent) over Yvette Herrell after redistricting.

In the 2024 presidential year he expanded that to about 138,000 votes (52.1 percent) against Herrell's roughly 127,000 (47.9 percent) — a margin of about 4 points or 11,000 votes.

In 2026 Vasquez defeated Republican Greg Cunningham — a Trump-endorsed Marine veteran and retired Albuquerque police officer, and a top National Republican Congressional Committee target — by approximately 37,000 votes (roughly 58.8 percent to 41.3 percent).

Vasquez's raw total dropped from his 2024 figure (about 124,000 versus 138,000).

The Republican total collapsed from 127,000 in 2024 and roughly 96,000 in 2022 down to the mid-80,000s.

The larger margin was produced primarily by the absence of Republican voters, not by a surge in Vasquez's support.

County-level patterns were consistent with differential turnout. Vasquez performed strongly in Doña Ana County and the Bernalillo County portion of the district; Republicans held relatively better in more rural, energy-producing counties such as Otero and Eddy.

Those differences track participation rates more closely than a wholesale shift among previously high-loyalty groups.

The turnout numbers did not emerge in a vacuum.

For most of 2026, the Republican Party of New Mexico (RPNM) spent its energy fighting itself rather than Democrats, and the central figure in that fight was its chair, Amy Barela.

Barela, an Otero County commissioner, succeeded former Congressman Steve Pearce as state chair in late 2024. In March 2026 she filed for re-election to her county commission seat — two minutes before a fellow Republican, Jonathan Emery, filed to challenge her.

A long-standing party rule requires a state officer to immediately vacate the party post when they file for an office that another Republican is also seeking.

Bernalillo County Republicans publicly demanded she step down; Sandoval County's party chair accused her of ignoring a rule that had been on the books for two decades. 

Barela refused, the party commissioned an outside review from a Dallas firm that cleared her, and her defenders — including executive director Leticia Muñoz — cast the push to remove her as a hostile takeover.

The dispute went to court. Three Republican candidates — gubernatorial hopeful Duke Rodriguez, lieutenant governor candidate Aubrey Blair Dunn and opponent Johnathan Emery — sued, alleging the party was not only flouting its rules but favoring certain candidates in contested primaries.

On May 27, District Judge Cindy Mercer issued a preliminary injunction barring Barela from serving as chair and prohibiting party leaders from backing one Republican over another in contested primaries, citing as evidence a party social media post that promoted only selected candidates. On June 2, Barela narrowly lost her commission primary to Emery — by 46 votes. On June 10, the New Mexico Supreme Court unanimously denied the party's appeal.

Then Barela on social media went onto the attack of this media outlet and its affiliates and a constant barrage of ongoing attacks on this journalist rather than accepting personal accountability for her actions and her loss.

Then, she announced on social media that she would run to get her old job as state chair back.

What followed was a summer of leadership paralysis.

First Vice Chair Mike Nelson took over on an interim basis. A State Central Committee meeting in Las Cruces on June 20 drew only about 160 members in person or by proxy — far short of the 358 needed for a quorum — after most northern New Mexico Republicans boycotted it. Northern Republicans called a rival meeting in Belen; the party called another in Albuquerque for late July. The split was explicitly regional: a coalition of southern and rural county officers backed Barela and the southern meeting sites, while one northern candidate for chair warned that her return would amount to southern New Mexico having "bullied their way to a chairmanship."

The practical result: heading into a general election, the state party had no elected chair.

One former local official summed up the situation after Election Day, calling the RPNM a "nonfunctioning party" that had no chairman and had poured its energy into internal fights.

Muñoz, Barela's ally, offered the mirror-image diagnosis: the counties that lost Republican House incumbents, she argued, had spent their time trying to remove Barela instead of turning out voters.

The infighting had concrete consequences on the ballot

The RPNM under Barela’s leadership failed to field candidates through the normal process for U.S. Senate, state auditor and state treasurer. 

Republicans were left scrambling for late write-in candidates: former oil and gas operator Larry Marker for Senate and Sam Kane for attorney general.

Northern Republicans blamed Barela directly for the failure to field several high-profile candidates for November.

The race for governor nearly lost a candidate, too — state Sen. Steve Lanier was disqualified from the GOP primary over a missed filing deadline.

Money followed the same pattern.

Haaland raised a record of roughly $19 million to about $2.5 million for Hull.

Even in the spring, Republican gubernatorial candidates had raised about one-tenth of what Democrats had. Critics after the election said the state party raised almost nothing and could not help Hull raise money.

Former GOP congressional candidate Mick Rich wrote that the oil and gas industry declined to fully back the legislative strategy or the gubernatorial nominee, suggesting donors walked away once their preferred primary candidate lost.

During the chair fight, one candidate claimed publicly that the party's donor base was heavily tied to oil and gas and that Barela had said the money would leave if she were not returned to the chair — a claim that could not be independently verified but that circulated widely among activists.

National Republicans, meanwhile, largely left Hull on his own. Trump never endorsed him, no major conservative outside group came to his aid, and a Democratic Governors Association–backed committee ran TV ads tying him to the president anyway.

From the start, the RPNM's civil war was fought in public.

In March, state Sen. Jim Townsend of Artesia published a lengthy Facebook post scolding Barela's critics; county chairs answered with posts calling her a hypocrite and warning her conduct would cost the party in November.

Sandoval County's GOP chair circulated infographics questioning the chair's neutrality, while the state party issued statements asking members whether they would stand with Barela or against the mission to flip New Mexico red.

After Election Day, the recriminations intensified.

Aubrey Blair Dunn, the former lieutenant governor candidate and one of the plaintiffs, posted on Facebook that Haaland owed her victory to the RPNM and named Pearce, Townsend and Barela among those responsible — arguing the party had run candidates too closely tied to Trump and pushed independents toward Democrats by attacking Republicans who criticized the president.

A graphic circulating among Republicans calls for firing the party's entire executive committee and holds it responsible for campaign transfers, mailers and messaging; its dollar figures have not been verified. Barela's defenders continue to argue that the effort to oust her was itself the distraction that sank Republicans.

The next round is already scheduled.

Officer elections for the next two-year term are set for Jan. 9 in Clovis — assuming the party can reach the quorum it has repeatedly failed to muster. Whether Barela seeks the chair again, and whether northern and southern factions show up in the same room, will shape whether the party enters 2028 rebuilt or still divided.

New Mexico's results were part of a national wave in which Democrats won control of the U.S. House.

In New Mexico, Democrats swept every statewide and congressional race and flipped four Republican-held state House seats — HD-7 (Los Lunas), HD-38 (Elephant Butte), HD-39 (Silver City) and HD-57 (Rio Rancho) — giving them 47 of 70 seats and a two-thirds supermajority. New Mexico has not elected a Republican statewide in a decade.

The environment worked against Republicans from the top down.

Two April polls put Trump's support in New Mexico at just 37 percent, and voters described the election as a referendum on the president and rising living costs. Exit polling and local commentary pointed to gas prices, affordability, tariffs and trade policy, and immigration enforcement as issues that energized Democrats.

Republican legislators pointed to the historical pattern of midterm losses for the president's party and predicted the pendulum would swing back.

Nationally, Republicans have begun their own round of blame, with some insiders privately faulting Trump for the scale of the losses in New Mexico the reasons are well beyond Trump. 

The single most important fact in the turnout data is that the missing Republican voters did not, for the most part, become Democratic voters.

They became non-voters.

Roughly 237,000 registered Republicans cast ballots in 2026. Had Republicans matched their 2022 participation rate of about 61 percent, the party would have banked tens of thousands of additional votes statewide — enough to cut deeply into, though not erase, Haaland's margin.

National analysis points the same direction.

Data scientist Lenny Bronner, studying detailed results from 13 states including New Mexico, estimated that about 75 percent of Democratic gains came from a turnout gap and only about 20 percent from Republicans switching sides. 

In his words, it looks like "more Trump voters who didn't vote Republican stayed home rather than switching.

Political scientist Michael McDonald likewise found that Trump's older voter base was more likely to sit out.

Which Republicans stayed home?

Voter files do not record ideology, so the answer requires inference — but several signals point toward the party's less ideological, more moderate and lower-engagement members:


They had no one to vote for down-ballot. In races where the party never fielded a nominee — U.S. Senate, auditor, treasurer — there was little reason for a casual Republican to show up beyond the governor's race.

The party's public face was its own feud. For months, the most visible RPNM activity was litigation, quorum fights and Facebook warfare. Mainstream Republicans who care more about crime, schools or the economy than party bylaws saw a party that could not govern itself — exactly the argument Democrats made in their own statements.

The candidate built for them was left alone. Hull ran an issues-focused campaign, kept Trump at arm's length and tried to court Democrats and independents. That positioning is designed to win moderate Republicans and swing voters — but without party money, national support or a functioning state organization, the campaign lacked the infrastructure to find and turn them out.

The Trump drag hit the middle hardest. Democrats spent heavily tying Hull to an unpopular president anyway. For moderate Republicans uneasy with Trump but unwilling to vote for a Democrat, skipping the election was the path of least resistance. Dunn's post-election critique — that the party drove away Republicans and independents who criticized the president — reflects this argument from inside the GOP.

Independents behaved the same way. Unaffiliated voters, now 28 percent of the electorate and growing, cast only about 16 percent of early ballots and turned out at roughly 32 percent overall. Many of them are former moderate Republicans or Republican-leaning voters, and their absence follows the same pattern.

The distinction matters. A voter who switches parties has to be persuaded back; a voter who stays home only has to be motivated to return.

As Bronner put it, those voters are easier for the GOP to win back — which is both a warning for Democrats and an opening for a reorganized Republican Party.

Several factors combined to produce the Republican participation decline:

No presidential race at the top of the ticket. Donald Trump has repeatedly demonstrated the ability to mobilize lower-propensity Republican and some independent voters who often sit out midterms; those voters were less present in 2026.

A referendum on the second Trump term. Concerns over cost of living, tariffs and immigration enforcement motivated Democratic voters while leaving portions of the Republican base less energized.

A state party in disarray; the Barela Effect- No elected chair, failed quorums, lawsuits, unfilled ballot slots and little money meant there was no coordinated effort to counter Democrats' early-vote advantage. Ego over party unity. 

Weaker local stakes. Competitive local races and residual energy from the post-2020 environment helped keep Republican turnout relatively stronger in 2022. Those conditions were weaker in 2026.

Independents also turned out at low rates. Meanwhile, the Democratic share of the overall registered electorate has declined in recent years while the independent share has grown, yet in this midterm the participation-rate advantage went to Democrats — the reverse of 2022.

The 2026 results do not require a permanent realignment to explain them. Statewide and district margins expanded largely because one side participated at a lower rate than it had four years earlier. If Republican and independent turnout returns closer to 2022 or 2024 levels in the next presidential cycle — particularly with a strong mobilizing figure at the top of the ticket — the arithmetic changes.

But whether that happens depends heavily on what the RPNM does in the next few months In New Mexico.

A party that resolves its leadership fight in January, recruits candidates for every statewide race and rebuilds a donor base can realistically bring stay-home Republicans back.

A party that carries the Barela fight and the Barela Effect into 2027 risks turning a one-cycle turnout dip into a habit.

Raw vote totals and party-specific turnout rates remain more transparent measures of what occurred than percentage margins alone — and they suggest the Republican problem in New Mexico in 2026 was less about persuasion than about showing up.

item.title: Weather Delays then Los Lunas Outlasts Alamogordo 13-6 5A Quarterfinal
item.description:
LOS LUNAS — Alamogordo waited out two weather delays and clawed within a point late, but No. 4 Los Lunas held on for a 13-6 win over the No. 5 Tigers on Saturday in the Class 5A state quarterfinals.

The loss ends Alamogordo's season at 7-5, the program's best finish in years and a big step forward in its first season in Class 5A.

The game was scheduled for a 1 p.m. kickoff but was pushed back by weather before it began. Once play started, neither team scored in the first quarter.

Los Lunas broke through with 2:03 left in the second quarter when Luke Cieremans threw a 37-yard touchdown pass to Andres Cordova. The extra point made it 7-0 at halftime.

Just as the second half was about to begin, a lightning strike sent both teams back off the field. Play didn't resume until about 3:35 p.m.

Alamogordo came out of the delay ready. With 1:29 left in the third quarter, senior Nathanael Cereceres hit Tristan Bowman for a 30-yard touchdown pass. Los Lunas blocked the extra point, keeping a 7-6 lead going into the fourth.

That blocked kick ended up deciding the game. Brad Mallory scored on a 2-yard run with 1:52 left to make it 13-6. The extra point missed, but Alamogordo couldn't get the tying score, and time ran out with the Tigers facing third-and-10.

Alamogordo dropped from 6A to 5A this fall and made the most of it. The Tigers finished 7-5 overall and 5-2 in District 2-5A, good for third in a league that includes state powers Roswell and Artesia.

The season didn't start smoothly. After opening with wins over Santa Fe (41-33) and at Goddard (28-27), Alamogordo lost to Clovis, Organ Mountain, Roswell and Artesia and sat at 2-4 at homecoming. From there the Tigers won four straight to finish the regular season 6-4, including a 23-14 win at Gadsden in which they ran for 372 yards.

They opened the playoffs with a 54-0 shutout of district rival Chaparral, then nearly upset Los Lunas on the road.

This was coach AJ Cisco's best season in at least six years. Going into the year, the Tigers had won a combined 18 games over the previous five seasons:

Last year, a 48-43 loss to Clovis on the final night of the regular season kept the Tigers out of the 6A playoffs. Before that season, local outlet 2nd Life Media wrote that a 6-4 record would be the program's best since 2011.

Los Lunas moves on to face No. 1 Roswell in the semifinals. The Coyotes beat Santa Fe 49-19 on Friday and have scored at least 42 points in eight straight games.

In the other semifinal, No. 3 Artesia meets No. 2 Piedra Vista. Artesia held off Gadsden 38-35 on Saturday, and Piedra Vista shut out Goddard 50-0.

The NMAA has the semifinals set for Nov. 20-21 and the state championship for Nov. 28. Sites and kickoff times have not been announced.

item.title: In Memory of Aundria Marcella Britt Schorn
item.description:
Aundria Marcella Britt Schorn, lovingly known to many as “Aundy,” passed away on November 6, 2026, surrounded by love.

Aundria was born on August 7, 1947, in Clovis, New Mexico, to Juanita Devoll and Joe Britt. In 1951, Aundria, her parents, and her three sisters moved to Roswell, New Mexico, where the girls grew up on the dairy where their father worked.

From a young age, Aundria developed a love for sewing and music. She first learned to play the accordion, followed by the organ and piano. Her love of music grew over the years, and she went on to play and sing in church. During her final days, she reflected fondly on those memories and spoke about how much she missed singing in the church.

Aundria also became an incredibly talented seamstress. In 1991, she opened Aundy’s Stitches in Alamogordo, New Mexico, where she did a little bit of everything but specialized in wedding and formal dresses. She was creative, crafty, and truly a jack of all trades. She enjoyed cross-stitching, making teddy bears, acrylic painting, quilting, and finding joy in creating things with her hands, especially for others.

Between 1967 and 1971, Aundria welcomed three children into the world: Dianna, Beverly, and Shane. Each went on to bless her with many grandchildren and even more great-grandchildren, all of whom she adored dearly.

In May 1995, Aundria married her best friend, Leo Schorn, in Alamogordo, New Mexico. In her final days, she spoke about their wedding day, recalling the dresses she had made for herself and her family, the kisses she and Leo shared (which she described as “passionate”), and the laughter they shared while dancing, despite neither of them knowing quite how to dance.

But her favorite wedding-day memory was sitting on the floor with three of her grandchildren, Danielle, Isaac, and Kimberly, sharing wedding cake all together.

Aundria and Leo enjoyed spending time together doing yard work and traveling in their travel trailer with all of their doggies. They also owned and operated Schorn’s Bookkeeping, where they worked side by side providing tax preparation and bookkeeping services for many years, until Leo's passing.

Aundria had a love for life's little joys. She adored elephants, baking, putting together puzzles, reading, watching movies, and matching her light switch covers to the theme of each room. She had the silliest sense of humor and made it her mission to make someone giggle in every room she entered.

Aundria will be remembered and missed for her many talents, her love of those around her, her silly sense of humor, and the countless memories she created with those fortunate enough to know and love her.

Aundria was preceded in death by her grandmother, Mollie Devoll, her parents Juanita and Joe Britt, her sister Gloria Turner, and her husband, Leo Schorn.

She is survived by her sisters, Mary Smith and Patsy Cates, her daughters, Dianna Bariou and husband John Bariou, Beverly Apticar and husband Nathan Apticar, her son, Shane Smith-Curry. Her grandchildren, Danielle Jones and husband Nick Jones, Chaler Smith-Curry, Isaac Luechtefeld and wife Raquel Luechtefeld, Kimberly Weddle, Sean Smith-Curry, Katie Brown and husband Bridger Brown. Her great grandchildren, Garrett Fralix, Rose Alt, Madilyn Weddle, Willow and Erik Wood, Enoch, Hannah, and Job Luechtefeld.

Family visitation will be on December 4, 2026 from 4:00pm - 7:00pm at Scenic Chapel in Alamogordo, New Mexico. Graveside service will be 10:00am December 5, 2026 at Immaculate Conception Catholic Cemetery in Alamogordo, New Mexico. In a small way of honoring Aundria, those who wish are welcome to wear purple to her services.

item.title: Zero Shovels, $180K Salary: Alamogordo’s Gang of Four Stalls the Work
item.description:
Broken Promises, High Salaries, and Zero Shovels: How the Gang of Four and a $180,000 Bureaucrat Are Starving Alamogordo’s Infrastructure and Driving Away the Workers Who Could Fix It

Alamogordo NM - For more than two years the Alamogordo City Commission staged a recruitment process that repeatedly delayed, derailed, and ultimately discarded a qualified local candidate who already held a Ph.D., had run the city successfully for roughly 28 months as acting manager, and had scored at the top of prior evaluations. In March 2026 the commission voted 7-0 to open contract negotiations with Dr. Stephanie Hernandez. Weeks later the same body reversed itself. A four-commissioner bloc—Josh Rardin, Stephen Burnett, Baxter Pattillo, and Al Hernandez—voted 4-3 to accept a settlement tied to an EEOC matter and end her tenure. They then installed Robert Stockwell, a former city manager the commission itself terminated by a 5-1 vote in 1997, through closed executive sessions and a consent-agenda path. The vote was 5-2. The process that produced him was neither the open national search the public was promised nor a transparent comparison of finalists.

Stockwell’s contract set a $180,000 base salary—above the range previously advertised and above the figures discussed for Hernandez—plus a $500 monthly vehicle allowance, immediate credit of 180 hours of paid time off, full benefits, and six months’ severance. First-year value exceeds $200,000; total compensation has been estimated in the $236,000–$242,000 range.

Recent permanent managers were paid far less: Brian Cesar roughly $130,000–$135,000, Maggie Paluch $120,000. The package was adapted from a draft employment agreement originally prepared for Hernandez, with her name struck through and Stockwell’s inserted, then sweetened. Commissioner Rardin later claimed the deal mirrored a 2012 interim consulting arrangement; city records show it does not.

Builders and developers were told the water-rate increases and new bond capacity would produce contracts, skilled jobs, and measurable growth.

Rates began rising in July 2024—the first increase since 2015—under a multi-year plan meant to support roughly $160 million in critical water and sewer repairs. Further adjustments followed in 2025.

The city locked in an initial roughly $28 million financing package.

The project list was concrete: tank rehabilitation, La Luz Reservoir work (infrastructure dating to 1914), citywide meter replacement, Granada Hills, the Alaska/Post Office district, Oregon Avenue Phase 2, White Sands Boulevard, and the Walker Road/Airport Road corridor—pipes and streets neglected for five to seven decades.

Under the prior acting administration those packages were described as shovel-ready or advancing, with engineering complete or nearly complete and funding identified. Oregon Phase 1, New York Avenue, 10th Street repairs, tank rehabs were already slotted and completed. But now nothing. 

Under Stockwell the forward motion stopped.

He has publicly blamed prior design work and ordered staff to hold new projects until they are “really ready,” even while the same on-call engineering firms remain on the city’s payroll for the assignments in question.

Oregon Phase 2, Granada Hills, White Sands and 10th, Walker Road and related water-and-road packages that had been scheduled for bidding have been paused.

Mayor’s-office announcements later in 2026 still listed several of the same projects as ready for competitive bids in the coming months; those bids have not appeared. Residents have absorbed successive rate increases. The contracts, the local payrolls, and the visible street work have not followed.

Roads are much worse then they were even 6 months ago and no progress but certain commissioners ensure golf course improvements moved forward. 

Local contractors who routinely perform comparable water, sewer, and paving work in Mescalero, Las Cruces, La Luz, and other nearby communities are left waiting or looking elsewhere.

Skilled crews and individual tradespeople are leaving Alamogordo for steadier employment.

When the city finally releases the backlog—if it does—the experienced local workforce that was supposed to execute the work may already be gone.

That is not economic development. It is a self-inflicted contraction: higher rates, idle capital, and a shrinking pool of people who know how to dig the trenches and lay the pipe.

Twenty-eight million dollars sits authorized. A bureaucracy headed by a city manager whose base pay alone is $180,000 has not converted that authorization into competitive bids or construction.

Closed-door executive sessions continue to shield performance reviews, settlements, and investigations from public view.

The four commissioners who engineered the leadership change—Rardin, Burnett, Pattillo, and Al Hernandez—own this failure and poor result.

They sold rate increases and bond capacity as the fuel for growth and good-paying local jobs. What the public has received is a higher-paid manager, delayed projects, lawsuits and settlements, and workers leaving town.

It is time the gang of four stops protecting the process and starts demanding results in the open.

Publish the closed door quarterly city manager evaluations. Release the records on why projects are held up. 

Put the designed and financed water, drainage, and road projects to bid. Fix the infrastructure.

That is the only outcome that matches what Alamogordo was told it would get. Everything short of that is a broken promise financed by ratepayers who are still waiting for the work. The public is demanding answers and the public has grown impatient.

item.title: FEMA and FCC Conduct Nationwide Emergency Alert System Test Today at 12:20 p.m. MT
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Radio and television stations across the country, including those serving Alamogordo and Otero County, will briefly interrupt programming today for a nationwide test of the Emergency Alert System. The test is scheduled for approximately 2:20 p.m. Eastern Time (12:20 p.m. Mountain Time) on Tuesday, November 17, 2026.

Federal Emergency Management Agency officials emphasized that the exercise is a routine, scheduled test required by law. FEMA is mandated under the IPAWS Modernization Act of 2015 to test public alert and warning capabilities at least once every three years. The last nationwide test occurred in 2023.

“This is only a test,” FEMA stated in advance of the event. “There is no secret emergency happening here. This is a routine check to ensure our public warning systems work when they are needed most.”

Unlike some previous tests, this one is limited to television and radio. Cell phones will not receive Wireless Emergency Alerts, and residents should not expect beeps, buzzes, or notifications on their phones.

During the test, normal programming on radio and television stations will pause for roughly one minute while the test message airs. The message will clearly identify itself as a test and state that no action is required by the public. Programming is expected to resume immediately afterward. The test message will be available in English and Spanish.

FEMA Administrator Cameron Hamilton said the tests are essential for readiness. “During an emergency, every second is crucial. FEMA’s alert and warning systems ensure that no second is wasted getting you the critical information needed to keep you safe. Operational tests like this allow us to identify and fix potential issues before an actual emergency occurs.”

Local listeners and viewers of KALHRadio.org other local radio and area television stations should expect the brief interruption around 12:20 p.m. today. Officials note that if a significant real-world emergency or severe weather event occurs, the test could be postponed to a backup date of December 3, 2026.

No personal action is required from the public. The Emergency Alert System does not collect personal data and is used solely to broadcast information.

For more information, visit FEMA’s 2026 Nationwide Emergency Alert System Test page at fema.gov.

item.title: Before tonight's vote, municipal league guidance weighs in on Alamogordo agenda dispute
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — When the Alamogordo City Commission takes up the question of Mayor Sharon McDonald's role in building meeting agendas tonight, commissioners will have more than the city's own procedural rules to consider. Guidance published by the New Mexico Municipal League speaks directly to two of the arguments in the dispute.

The commission meets at 6:30 p.m. in the Donald E. Carroll City Commission Chambers at City Hall, 1376 E. Ninth St.

As Alamogordo Town News reported Saturday, City Manager Robert Stockwell has asked commissioners to clarify Rule 5(a) of Resolution 2018-08, the commission's meeting procedures. The rule says the city clerk "shall consult with the City Manager and the Mayor" when preparing agendas, but it says nothing about timing, form or whether the mayor approves drafts.

McDonald has asked City Clerk Rachel Hughs and Stockwell for a preliminary draft of each agenda, time to review it and meet with them before publication, and a say in any later removal or significant change. She has written that the request is about being prepared as presiding officer, not about interfering with administration, and she has not claimed veto power over items.

Stockwell says the extra review step would push the staff deadline for agenda items from noon Tuesday back to the previous Friday. He says earlier mayors sometimes sat in on agenda reviews but never held approval authority. Our research in speaking with previous city managers and mayors show the previous 4 mayors and city managers reviewed the agenda prior to publication with the mayor either by email or in person and they did it under the present timeframe as precedent. If Mr Stockwell cannot manage timelines established over 4 past administrations then his time management skills need evaluated. His closed door evaluations by the commission each quarter need to be made public as well. 

Stockwell also points out that the full commission votes to adopt the agenda at the start of every meeting, this is counter to municipal league guidance.

McDonald says pre-publication meetings were routine under former mayors Susie Galea, Richard Boss and Susan Payne, and Payne has backed her account, though not always via in person meetings. 

The New Mexico Municipal League's newsletter, The Municipal Reporter, runs an "Ask a Clerk" column for clerks and local officials.

One 2025 column answered whether a governing body needs an agenda item to approve its own agenda. The League's answer was no.

The column made three points that bear on tonight's discussion:

The agenda vote may not be the safeguard it appears to be. The column says a standing "approval of agenda" item is unnecessary and runs contrary to the New Mexico Open Meetings Act. Under that law, the agenda must be prepared and made public at least 72 hours before the meeting, and some matters, such as zoning hearings, require published or mailed notice even earlier. The column asks what a governing body would do if its agenda-approval motion failed after notices had gone out and residents had shown up. Alamogordo's agendas include an "Approval of Agenda" item, and Stockwell has cited that vote as the commission's check on the agenda.

The mayor runs the meeting. The column says state law makes the mayor the presiding officer of governing body meetings in every form of municipal government. That gives the mayor authority to move items around on the agenda during the meeting so it runs efficiently. Some cities, the column notes, keep the agenda-approval item mainly so items can be rearranged, which it says the mayor can already do.

Local rules govern the details. The column says many cities spell out agenda creation and approval in their own rules of procedure, and that cities with adopted rules should follow them as written.

The column closes by citing Robert's Rules of Order in Brief, 3rd edition, which describes the presiding officer as the person who keeps order, enforces the rules and decides who speaks.

The League column addresses the mayor's authority during a meeting. It does not say whether a mayor should review agenda drafts before they are published, which is the heart of the Alamogordo disagreement.

On that point, the column's own advice sends the question back home. Alamogordo has adopted rules, and Rule 5(a) requires the clerk to consult the mayor. The question before commissioners is what "consult" means: Stockwell's narrower reading, in which existing manager-clerk review already satisfies the rule, or a broader more recognized reading statewide is  that it gives the mayor input while the agenda is being drafted.

Stockwell has said that if the commission finds McDonald's request appropriate, Rule 5(a) should be amended to spell out the process.

State statute adds context on both sides. Under NMSA 3-14-10, the mayor presides and carries out duties the commission assigns, with a commissioner's powers and vote, but no separate administrative authority. Daily administration belongs to the city manager under NMSA 3-14-13 and 3-14-14.

The city charter, Article VIII, Section 2, names the mayor presiding officer and the representative and voice of the city.

The League offers help to cities working through these questions. Its contact for the topic is Rebecca Martinez at rmartinez@nmml.org or 505-690-3278.

Closed-door complaint. Commissioners will go into executive session to consider a complaint concerning Stockwell and Community Development Director Shelley Dowhanik-Baron, an item McDonald placed on the agenda. A possible open-session vote could authorize an independent investigation. The packet does not identify the complainant or the allegations.

Fairgrounds parking lot. A closed session on the possible sale of the property, with a possible vote afterward. No buyer or price has been named.

Billboard moratorium. Resolution 2026-38, on the consent agenda, would pause new off-premise billboards and electronic conversions for six months while the city updates its sign rules. It would be the city's seventh such moratorium since 2018.

Library grant. Acceptance of a $10,532.02 State Grants-in-Aid award from the New Mexico Department of Cultural Affairs.

December schedule. Stockwell proposes merging the two December meetings into one on Dec. 8.

Residents who want to speak during public comment must sign up with the city clerk; the usual limit is three minutes. To sign up individuals must sign the list prior to 6:30.

The full agenda packet is posted on the city's website. For disability accommodations, call the City Clerk's Office at 575-439-4100 at least 48 hours ahead.

Alamogordo Town News will update this story with the commission's decisions after tonight's meeting.

Sources: Alamogordo Town News, "Alamogordo commission to weigh mayor's agenda role, closed-door complaint against city manager," Nov. 14, 2026; New Mexico Municipal League, The Municipal Reporter, "Ask a Clerk," 2025 issue, page 5.
