item.title: Alamogordo commission settles agenda dispute, but clash over city manager inquiry erupts
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — A months-long tug-of-war over the mayor's role in setting the City Commission's agenda ended quietly Tuesday night with a unanimous vote allowing her a seat at the table following past precedent and municipal league recommendations.

Then a vote to look into an anonymous complaint against City Manager Robert Stockwell first passed then turned the end of the meeting into an open confrontation between Stockwell and Mayor McDonald, with 5 of the men on the commission  voting against an inquiry into the behavior of Mr Stockwell per an anonymous letter that was sent to multiple press outlets and the city of Alamogordo Commission by a staff member anonymously for justified fear of retaliation. 

The agenda item, titled "Consider and act upon the mayor's role in city commission agenda process," was placed on the agenda by Stockwell, not the mayor. He said a memo from the mayor asking to review draft agendas, and to be consulted on any changes afterward, went beyond past practice and could keep items off the agenda when they came in late. In a long and heated debate the conversation moved forward. 

The mayor read written statements from former Mayors Susan Payne and Susie Galea, former Mayor Pro Tem Nadia Sykes, and former City Manager Stephanie Hernandez. All of them described regular meetings where past mayors went over draft agendas before they were published. The mayor cited Resolution 2018-08, Rule 5A, which says the city clerk "shall consult with the city manager and mayor" when preparing the agenda.

"I am not asking to control the agenda, interfere with administrative duties, or prevent any commissioner from bringing forward an item," she said. She added that she had not been invited to an agenda meeting since Stockwell started on July 1. 

Stockwell said he had no objection to the mayor attending staff's agenda review, held at 2 p.m. on the Tuesday before each meeting. He said the problem was the request to see draft items and backup material ahead of that meeting, and to approve changes after it. Staff noted that department heads often turn items in as late as Tuesday night, the day of the review.

Some commissioners questioned whether the mayor should have any extra role. Rardin noted that Alamogordo has a "weak mayor" form of government. "All seven of us sitting up here have the exact same authority," he said. Tapley and Tardin read the mayor's memo as a directive to the city manager, which she denied. "It was never meant to be a demand," she said.

The commission voted 7-0 for a motion by Commissioner Robinson, seconded by Commissioner Hernandez, that the mayor will attend the Tuesday 2 p.m. meeting to review the agenda only and follow the process that has been precedent for over a decade and if which Stockwell has not followed with an invitation to attend until the mayor requested it. The mayor will now attend the meetings per the vote of 7 to 0. 

Vote on complaint against city manager sparks confrontation

After a closed executive session, the commission took up a complaint, brought forward by the mayor, about the city manager and the community development director. The commission directed Human Resources Director Michelle Osborne to have an independent party conduct a limited inquiry and report back at a future executive session.

Commissioner Burnett made the motion "as much as I don't want to do this," calling it due diligence. Mayor Pro Tem Rardin seconded it but called the inquiry "unwarranted due to the fact that it's anonymous." The motion first appeared to pass, 5-2.

Stockwell then asked to speak. He waived his right to have the matter kept in executive session and asked the mayor, "Who initiated this witch hunt?" He said he wanted to know exactly what he was accused of. He tied the complaint to an anonymous letter sent to commissioners on Oct. 5 that he said had been widely circulated and picked up by local media as the letter was sent to multiple local media outlets. Mr. Stockwell took offense the letter was reported in local press and that the mayor placed a discussion of rather to investigate it into the agenda.

This media outlet along with our sister radio station received a copy of the letter and reported that an accusation has been made concerning the city manager and a staff members’ behavior. This media outlet in order to protect the privacy of the director in question did not provide the name nor position of that director. That information was later leaked as a part of another complaint filed against the city and via staff members notifying the news outlet of inquiries as to rather they were offended by actions. 

This media outlet provided a commentary based upon paid staff members of the city contacting us and ran a story with comment from Mr. Stockwell to ensure fairness in reporting.

The reporting included: 

Commentary: Same Pattern, Same Silence: Potential Sexual Harassment at Alamogordo City Hall Demands Answers
and 

Letter on City Hall Workplace Concerns Reaches Commission, Press and Former City Leaders; City Manager Responds

"The commission has one employee," Stockwell said. "Why didn't you sit down with me?" He called the letter "garbage" and questioned spending public money on a complaint from someone "not even willing to put their name behind something."

The mayor said she put the item on the agenda as due diligence, not as an accusation, which is exactly what the public expects for transparency purposes. She said HR had told her city employees cannot investigate the city manager, so the work would have to be done by an outside party. "If we're investigating the employees that serve you, you're not above that either," she said. Stockwell said she was linking unrelated matters.

Citing Rule 21 of the commission's rules, Rardin asked for a revote so he could change his vote to support the city manager. A longtime commissioner, Hernandez  who served with Stockwell before also backed him, saying any concern with the city's one employee should be handled by sitting down with him "like adults."

What the mayor did by placing it on the agenda was exactly what the public would expect a discussion, proof of a discussion by it being placed on the agenda and transparency.

Five of the 6 men on the commission took offense to even having the discussion which was expected. The item was put to revote and 5 of the 7 commissioners voted to change their direction and not investigate Stockwell coming to his defense rather than allow an independent investigation. 

Osborne told the commission that an independent reviewer looked at an employee grievance (that grievance was filed by former project manager Justen Boyle) that mentioned the city manager. The reviewer found no conflict of interest and said Stockwell can hear the grievance himself. That meeting is set for Thursday at noon with Mr Boyle who has been terminated by the city under questionable circumstances and who has potentially filed an FMLA and or EEOC complaint for wrongful termination. 

The commission took no action on the sale of the fairgrounds parking lot, which was discussed in closed session.

Golf course: The city signed an agreement with Maximum Golf to take over running the golf course. The handoff happens in December and is to be finished by Dec. 31.

City attorney: Several months of recruiting did not produce a city attorney, so the city will issue a request for proposals to law firms in early December, open for 30 days. The mayor and two commissioners will sit on the review committee. Stockwell hopes to bring a contract to the commission by mid- to late January.

Projects: Fire Station No. 2 should be done once its driveways are paved, possibly by late next week.

The $2.2 million refurbishment of the Callahan water tank is complete

Bids for the (only major project to be released under Stockwell’s leadership since assuming the helm on July 1st), the Alamo Aquatic Center will close Dec. 15.

Coming soon: A billboard ordinance should come to the commission within about a month. An extraterritorial jurisdiction ordinance and the drainage master plan are expected in January. The "Let's Grow Alamo" comprehensive plan is on schedule for spring 2027.

Streets: Staff has started talks with the state Department of Transportation about having the state rebuild White Sands Boulevard and then hand it over to the city. 

A road survey found Alamogordo's streets are in typical condition for U.S. cities. "Our roads are bad, but the good news is, everybody else's are bad too," Stockwell said making light of the nation’s infrastructure failures.

The referenced survey has not been released to the public but an IPRA has been filed seeking what Mr. Stockwell referenced.

If the survey Stockwell referenced was a prior survey from 2022 it supports viewing Alamogordo’s roads as average/typical for a city its size—meaning the problems are real and shared with many other communities, driven by funding and maintenance realities—while New Mexico as a state is on the weaker end of U.S. rankings. The city’s 2022 assessment provides the local data foundation, and TRIP reports supply the strongest comparative state/national context. Specific block-by-block or exact PCI numbers would require the full city report or commission presentation materials of which were not released as a part of the city mangers report. 

A traffic study is underway on whether to close the Mountain View Bridge as part of the Oregon Avenue Phase Two project.

Bonita Lake: The lake remains open for fishing, but other access is limited because of runoff and debris. Stockwell said shoreline access should be safe by next summer, with long-term decisions involving Lincoln County and the state still a couple of years away.

The commission also unanimously combined its two December meetings into one on Dec. 8.

Resident Russell Davis said the restored Dudley School in Chihuahuita is still not open as a true community center. Its kitchen is unfinished, and it is not listed on the city's website.

In response, one commissioner said most of the commission had never been allowed to use the building, and Stockwell said it is now available to anyone who requests it.

Beth Crab criticized the agenda of the agenda discussion debate and the mayors role as a waste of time and that the city needs to manage under past precedent. She also questioned paying a city manager about $200,000 a year when the city's interim manager had cost much less.

The meeting adjourned abruptly with several of the male commissioners visibly agitated by the tone and questioning of a city manager in a defensive position as city infrastructure projects continue to be delayed without question by a majority of the commissioners.

item.title: From "The Dr. Is In" with Dr. Stephanie Hernandez “Mayors Agenda Request Blown Out of Proportion”
item.description:
Dr. Stephanie Hernandez says a city commission discussion this week over Mayor Sharon McDonald's role in the agenda process was "blown out of proportion," and that the mayor asked for nothing more than what city policy already calls for and has been established practice for years. 

Hernandez made the remarks on her segment "The Dr. Is In" in conversation with Anthony Lucero. The full comments can be heard on KALHRadio.org.

The issue came before commissioners at Tuesday night's meeting after McDonald sent an email asking to review draft agendas with the city manager and city clerk before they are published

See related story:

https://2ndlifemediaalamogordo.town.news/g/alamogordo-nm/n/398582/alamogordo-commission-settles-agenda-dispute-clash-over-city-manager

Hernandez said she read the email as "a reasonable request to understand the issues and ask questions on behalf of the citizens she represents. Nothing more."

She pointed to Resolution 2018-08, which she said directs that the city clerk shall consult with the city manager and the mayor.

"Shall consult, not may consult, and not occasionally consult," Hernandez said. "This isn't new."

Hernandez said she has taken part in many agenda reviews herself and described them as brief and productive.

"No mayor ever approved or removed agenda items," she said. "They sought clarification and prepared themselves to lead an informed discussion."

She added that any commissioner who asked for the same opportunity was given it, even though the resolution does not require it. "That's just simple good communication and professional management," she said.

"So why has something we've done for years suddenly become controversial?"

Hernandez argued that because the mayor presides over commission meetings and represents the entire city, her job goes beyond running the meeting to understanding the issues and guiding the discussion. 

She said there were times when McDonald appeared to be the only elected official who had thoroughly read the agenda reports beforehand, and that a standing agenda review on a set day and time is "simply good operational practice."

Hernandez said what she found "particularly troubling" was that the city manager indicated he did not appreciate the mayor's tone, but raised the matter before the full commission rather than with McDonald directly.

"If you disagree with someone's tone, especially one of your bosses, wouldn't the professional approach be to have a conversation?" she asked.

Instead, she said, something that could have been resolved between the manager and the mayor became a public discussion that "frankly felt more like an ambush."

Hernandez said the response pointed to "a clear alliance" on the commission that, in her view, seems more interested in challenging the mayor than working with her. She did not name individual commissioners.

She said McDonald repeatedly clarified during the meeting that she was not seeking additional authority or control over the agenda, but that "that narrative kept being pushed."

Hernandez closed by framing the dispute around residents.

"Everything done in local government is on behalf of the citizens," she said. "So why is helping the mayor become better informed to lead a more meaningful discussion on behalf of those citizens met with such resistance? That speaks volumes."

"We talk about leadership and collaboration," she added, "but those principles mean very little if we can't demonstrate them in something as basic as preparing for a meeting."

Dr. Stephanie Hernandez's full conversation with Anthony Lucero is available at KALHRadio.org and on YouTube per the link above in the article.

item.title: Cut Your Own Christmas Tree: Lincoln National Forest Permits Now Available for $10
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Families across Otero and Lincoln counties can once again skip the tree lot and head into the high country. The Lincoln National Forest is selling Christmas tree permits for the 2026 holiday season, allowing households to select and cut their own tree on public land for $10.

Permits are sold online through Recreation.gov, where a $2.50 transaction fee is added at checkout, and in person at three Lincoln National Forest offices, where no online fee applies. Online sales continue through December 31. In-person sales end December 24.

The program runs from mid-November through the end of December, giving late celebrators and anyone who simply wants to extend the season a window that stretches past Christmas Day.

Each household is limited to one tree. Trees must generally stand under 10 feet tall; anyone wanting a taller tree needs a special permit, which must be obtained in person at a forest office.

Cutting is allowed only in designated areas. The forest publishes maps and a cutting guide on its website so permit holders can confirm before they leave home that they will be on national forest land, inside an open harvest area, and not on private property or in a closed section of the forest.

Every small tree a family carries out is one less competing for water, light and space in an overcrowded stand.

The permit program is more than a holiday tradition. According to the Forest Service, removing small-diameter trees is a forest management tool. Thinning dense stands reduces competition among the remaining trees, lowers the risk of disease and insect infestation, improves wildlife habitat and helps keep forest density in check.

The height limit serves the same goal from the other direction: it steers harvesters toward small trees and leaves larger, more ecologically valuable trees standing.

Fourth graders who hold an Every Kid Outdoors pass are eligible for a free Christmas tree permit. The federal program gives fourth-grade students and their families free access to public lands for the school year, and the tree permit is one of its seasonal benefits. Families claiming the free permit online should expect the Recreation.gov processing fee to still apply.

Currently there are several lawsuits in various forms to include in the appeals process against the owner alleging violations of New Mexico consumer laws and other allegations including failure to properly maintain the park.

Some park residents are now in discussion about filing a class action suit against the owner seeking compensatory and punitive damages for issues associated with the park. Although none of the claims in the lawsuits have been adjudicated at this time, they are examples of issues and litigation that mobile home park residents are facing not only in Alamogordo, but across New Mexico and the United States. 

Out-of-state private equity and corporations are buying mobile home parks, increasing rents, failing to maintain parks, eliminating services and amenities all in the name Of increasing profits to owners.

item.title: Alamogordo Public Schools Earns National Award for Athlete Safety
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. (Nov. 18, 2026) — Alamogordo Public Schools has received the National Athletic Trainers' Association's Safe Sports School Award, a national honor given to secondary schools that take exemplary steps to keep student-athletes safe.

The district announced the recognition Wednesday, crediting close cooperation among its Health Services Department, Athletics Department, coaches and athletic trainers.

"The safety and well-being of our student-athletes is a priority for our district," Superintendent Michael Crabtree said. "This recognition reflects the dedication of our athletic trainers, coaches, health services staff, and administrators who work together every day to provide a safe environment for our students."

To earn the designation, schools must meet a set of rigorous criteria set by NATA. Among them:

Planning: building a sound athletic health care administrative system and developing and rehearsing emergency action plans tailored to each venue.

Physicals and facilities: providing or coordinating pre-participation physical exams, promoting safe practice and competition facilities, and keeping a permanent, fully equipped area to evaluate and treat injured athletes.

Equipment and prevention: properly selecting, fitting and maintaining athletic equipment, and adopting injury and illness prevention strategies, including protocols for weather and environmental conditions.

Care and education: providing injury intervention, facilitating psychosocial consultation and nutrition counseling, and educating athletes and parents about the benefits and risks of playing sports.

Athletic Director Alan Edmondson said the honor comes with obligations.

"Receiving this award is not just a feather in our cap, but also an ongoing responsibility," Edmondson said. "We will continue to uphold these high standards and look for new ways to enhance the safety of our athletic programs."

Head Athletic Trainer David Maldonado pointed to the partnership between his staff, school nurses, coaches and administrators.

"Winning the Safe Sports School Award validates the comprehensive safety web we have built together," Maldonado said. "It takes a dedicated team to provide standard-setting care, and we are thrilled that NATA has recognized our collective work."

NATA will send the district an official banner to hang at Alamogordo High School marking the achievement.

Founded in 1950, the National Athletic Trainers' Association is the professional membership group for certified athletic trainers and others who support the profession. It has more than 45,000 members worldwide.

item.title: Outgoing committee will choose New Mexico GOP leaders before counties seat new members, rules challenge notes
item.description:
ALBUQUERQUE — The members of the Republican Party of New Mexico's State Central Committee who will elect the party's next chairman on Jan. 9 are the outgoing committee, not the one county Republicans are set to choose later that month — a sequence that is now drawing questions inside the party.

Under the published schedule, the current State Central Committee (SCC) will elect RPNM's state officers on Jan. 9, 2027. County parties will then hold their organizational conventions between Jan. 16 and Jan. 31, when they elect new county central committees, county officers and the representatives who will sit on the next SCC.

The timing was raised in a Nov. 15 email exchange involving party member Gary Person, in which another Republican asked why outgoing SCC members were voting on new leadership and whether selecting the new SCC should come first.

"The existing rules explain how this is permitted," Person wrote in reply. "They do not explain the leadership's decision to schedule the elections in this order."

Person's analysis, which cites the party's Uniform State Rules (USRs), concludes that the schedule does not appear to break any rule.

USR 2-1-4(A) requires the SCC to elect state officers at an organizational meeting called between Nov. 15 and Jan. 15 following the biennial general election. The Jan. 9 date falls inside that window, and the rule does not require that the committee be newly elected before it votes.

County reorganizations, by contrast, are governed by USR 3-2-1(C), which requires organizational conventions in odd-numbered years but does not say they must precede the state officer election. And under USR 3-3-1(C), county-elected SCC members serve two years "or until their successors are selected and qualified," meaning members chosen in 2025 keep their votes until replacements qualify in 2027.

The roster for the January vote is also locked. USR 1-3-1(B)(i) bars changes to the SCC membership list once an official meeting call is issued, and the call for the Jan. 9 meeting went out Nov. 4.

Person argues that the rules apply a different logic at the county level. USR 3-1-4(A) requires each newly constituted county central committee to elect its county officers immediately after the new committee is selected — new members first, new leadership second. The state leadership rules contain no equivalent language.

"There is a clear representational argument" for having counties go first, Person wrote, since that would let newly chosen SCC members pick the chairman and officers who will lead them for the next two years. But he acknowledged that "the scheduling difference alone does not establish a rules violation."

Person said the practical effect of the dates is that the state election is completed by the existing SCC before county reorganization begins, but that without an explanation from party leadership, the reason for choosing those dates cannot be established.

The sequencing question is one of four issues Person raised in a Nov. 14 letter to Mr. VanDyke requesting a written determination from the party's Rules Committee:

Timing of the call. USR 2-1-4(A) sets a Nov. 15 – Jan. 15 window, but the official call was issued Nov. 4, eleven days before the window opened. Person asked whether the rule governs when the call is issued or only when the meeting is held, and what corrective action would be needed if the call was premature.

Candidate eligibility. USR 1-2-1(C) sets a 90-day Republican registration requirement, but the candidate self-nomination form reportedly requires 12 months of continuous registration. Citing USR 1-5-2(A), which prohibits suspending the rules, Person asked what adopted rule authorizes the longer requirement and whether the form should be corrected before nominations close Dec. 7.

Observer access. The call allows SCC members, qualified proxies and non-SCC officer candidates to attend, but does not expressly provide for other registered Republicans to observe. Person asked which rule prohibits non-voting observers and whether the Rules Committee could recommend allowing them, subject to registration, security and seating limits.

County representation. With the SCC roster frozen and county elections scheduled after Jan. 9, Person asked how the sequence ensures proper county representation, particularly if the call was issued early.

"With nominations closing on December 7, timely clarification is essential to protect qualified candidates, ensure proper representation, and maintain transparency in electing our party's leadership," Person wrote.

The January election caps a turbulent year for the state party. A court order removed former chair Amy Barela from her post, and the New Mexico Supreme Court denied the party's appeal in June. A June 20 SCC meeting called to fill the vacancy failed to reach quorum.

item.title: Want to Lead the New Mexico GOP? Here’s How Any Republican Can Run for State Party Office
item.description:
Self-nomination forms for the eight statewide party offices are due by 5 p.m. Dec. 7. Here’s what each job does, who can run, and how the vote works.

November 19, 2026 · Albuquerque by Journalist Chris Edwards 

The Republican Party of New Mexico (RPNM) is taking candidates for its top leadership posts for 2027–2028. Any registered Republican in the state who meets the requirements can run, whether they are a longtime county officer or a precinct volunteer who has never sought party office. Change begins from the ground up!

The party’s 2027 Self-Nomination Form lists eight offices: State Chair, First Vice Chair, Second Vice Chair, Secretary, Treasurer, and a Vice Chair for each of New Mexico’s three congressional districts.

The completed form must be received by RPNM before 5:00 p.m. on Monday, December 7, 2026. Mailed forms count only if they arrive by then.

This year’s vote comes after a hard stretch for the party. In 2026, a dispute over whether the sitting chair, Amy Barela broke party rules by running in a contested Republican primary ended in a court order removing her. She attempted to change those very rules and ignored them. Several State Central Committee meetings called to choose a replacement then failed to reach quorum. Whoever wins in December will serve a full two-year term covering 2027 and 2028. The party is fractured and is no longer welcoming many different factions. Under present leadership and staff there continues to be infighting, calling those that don’t toe the leadership line RINOs and an attitude of no inclusion - the New Mexico big GOP tent is not Ronald Reagan’s GOP tent. 

Who can run

The self-nomination form asks every candidate to affirm that they:

Are a registered Republican now, and have been continuously registered as a Republican in New Mexico forat least twelve months, beginning before November 4, 2026

Are a full-time New Mexico resident

Will pay their own way, including any RPNM or RNC fees, travel, food and lodging

Will make every effort to attend state conventions, county conventions, called meetings and related events in full

Agree that their contact information can be released to candidates, the media and others

Will follow the RPNM Uniform State Rules (USRs)

Have read and understand the duties of the office they are seeking, as laid out in USR 2-1-4

The party’s general rules for holding party office (USR 1-2-1 and 1-2-2) also require party officers to be registered Republicans who live at their registered address. An officer who changes party registration or moves out of the area automatically resigns.

Two conflict-of-interest rules matter in particular. State officers may not publicly endorse one Republican over another in a primary (USR 1-4-3).

And if a state officer files for public office in a race where another Republican has also filed, the officer must step down from party office immediately (USR 1-4-4).

That second rule is the one at the center of the 2026 lawsuit over the chairmanship and created significant party division costing Republican unity across New Mexico in 2026.

How to apply: step by step

Read the rules. The Uniform State Rules (the version adopted Sept. 6, 2025) are posted at newmexico.gop/usr. Article 2, and USR 2-1-4 in particular, sets out each office and its duties.

Fill out the 2027 Self-Nomination Form. Check the office you are seeking. Print your name, email, mailing address, city, ZIP code, primary phone and cell phone clearly, then sign and date the form.

Attach a letter of interest, résumé or personal bio. The party says it will share this material with the public and with the State Central Committee, the body that votes, by email no later than December 9, 2026. RPNM says it will not edit submissions, so proofread yours before you send it.

Get the form to the party by 5 p.m. Dec. 7. You can email it to Kathleen@gopnm.org, hand-deliver it, or mail it to: Republican Party of New Mexico, 5150 San Francisco Rd NE #A, Albuquerque, NM 87109. The party secretary checks each candidate’s registration and the date the form was received.

Campaign to State Central Committee members. Rank-and-file Republicans do not vote in this election. Members of the State Central Committee do.

Questions can go to RPNM headquarters at (505) 298-3662, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., or to contact@gopnm.org.

Who votes: the State Central Committee

Under USR 2-1-1, the State Central Committee (SCC) is the party’s governing body, with general supervision and control of its political affairs. It has hundreds of members. Membership comes from several sources:

Members elected by county. Each county gets one, plus one more for every 1,000 votes (or major fraction of 1,000) its voters cast for the Republican nominee for governor in the most recent gubernatorial election.

County party officers. Up to five per county.

Republican officeholders. Incumbents in the federal, statewide and legislative offices listed in the rules (judges excepted).

National committee members. New Mexico’s Republican National Committeeman and National Committeewoman.

Affiliated groups. Three members each from the Young Republicans, the College Republicans and the New Mexico Federation of Republican Women.

Current and former leaders. All former state chairs and former national committee members, the sitting state officers, and the chairs of the State Finance Committee and the Advisory State Rules Committee.

Quorum: Under USR 2-1-5, the SCC can do business only when at least two-thirds of its members, representing at least two-thirds of the counties, are present in person or by proxy. In 2026 several meetings fell short of that bar, so attendance in December will matter.

How the vote works

USR 2-1-4 says state officers are elected at an SCC meeting called between November 15 and January 15 after each general election. The official call for the meeting sets its date and location, and the rules require written notice at least 10 days ahead.

The statewide offices of chair, two vice chairs, secretary and treasurer are elected by the full SCC.

The three congressional district vice chairs are chosen in two stages. First, the SCC members from each district caucus together and nominate one candidate by secret ballot, or by voice vote if only one person is running. Then the full SCC votes to confirm or reject each nominee by majority, which counts as election at-large.

All officers take office the day after they are elected. They serve two years, or until a successor is elected or appointed.

What each officer does, and why it matters

A state party is not the government. It is the volunteer organization that recruits and supports candidates, raises money, trains county parties, runs conventions and pre-primary nominating events, and speaks for Republicans across the state. The eight state officers run that organization between SCC meetings. Under USR 2-1-4(E), each of them is automatically a member of both the SCC and the State Executive Committee (SEC), the smaller body that handles party business between meetings.

State Chair

The chair is the party’s chief executive and its most visible spokesperson. Under USR 2-1-4(F), the chair:

Presides over SCC meetings and calls them, with proper noticeSets the two-week window in which counties hold party officer and delegate electionsAppoints committees and assistants, plus 15 to 30 members of the State Executive Committee, who serve at the chair’s pleasureCalls a county’s organizational convention if the county fails toHires an executive director together with the SECSubmits an annual party budget by November 30 and approves any spending outside itMakes sure party property and records pass to the next chair

The chair also leads the SEC. With a majority vote of the SEC, the chair can declare a county chair’s office vacant if that county chair refuses to call a required meeting. The chair can be paid: a compensation committee made up of the other elected state officers and the national committee members may recommend an annual salary plus expenses, which the SCC approves or changes.

Why it matters: The chair sets the party’s strategy, controls its staff and budget, and is the public face of New Mexico Republicans going into the 2028 election cycle.

First Vice Chair

The first vice chair acts as chair whenever the chair is absent. If the chair’s office becomes vacant, the first vice chair must call an SCC meeting within 30 days to elect a permanent replacement. If the chair is away, the first vice chair can also be given authority to approve spending outside the budget.

Why it matters: As 2026 showed, this office can end up leading the party with little warning.

Second Vice Chair

The second vice chair acts for the chair when both the chair and the first vice chair are absent. If the chair’s office becomes vacant and the first vice chair is also absent, the second vice chair must call the meeting to fill it.

Why it matters: It is the second backup for party leadership and adds another voice on the Executive Committee.

Congressional District Vice Chairs (CD 1, CD 2, CD 3)

Under USR 2-1-4(I), the three district vice chairs carry out duties the chair assigns. Each one represents one of New Mexico’s three U.S. House districts.

Why it matters: New Mexico covers a lot of ground, from Albuquerque’s metro area (CD 1), to the southern half of the state (CD 2), to the north and the Navajo Nation (CD 3). The district vice chairs are how each region gets a seat at the leadership table, and in practice they often coordinate the county parties in their districts.

Secretary

Under USR 2-1-4(J), the secretary keeps the minutes of SCC and SEC meetings, prepares and sends meeting notices with the chair, and keeps a list of the party’s real and intellectual property. The secretary also serves as secretary of the Executive Committee and, under the self-nomination process, checks candidates’ registration and filing dates.

Why it matters: Meeting notices and records decide whether party actions are valid. That has come up repeatedly in recent disputes over meeting calls and quorum.

Treasurer

The treasurer performs the duties the chair and the law require. In practice that means handling the party’s money and its campaign-finance compliance. The rules bar the same person from serving as both chair and treasurer. If the treasurer’s office becomes vacant, the chair names a temporary replacement and the SCC holds an election within 30 days. The Executive Committee must also get an annual audit within 60 days after the fiscal year ends.

Why it matters: The treasurer is responsible for keeping the party’s books accurate, legal and audit-ready and transparent. 

Vacancies and removal

If an office other than chair or treasurer becomes vacant, the State Executive Committee fills it, and the SCC confirms the appointment at its next meeting. Any officer can be removed by a two-thirds vote of members present in person at a properly called meeting attended by at least 51% of the membership.

Proxies do not count for a removal vote.

item.title: Want to Lead the New Mexico Democratic Party? Here’s How State Party Officers Are Chosen
item.description:
The Democratic Party of New Mexico elects its next slate of state officers in spring 2027. Here’s what each job does, who votes, and how Democrats around the state can get involved.

November 19, 2026 · Albuquerque by Journalist Chris Edwards 

The Democratic Party of New Mexico (DPNM) will choose its statewide party leadership for the next two years in the spring of 2027. The officers elected in April 2025 (Chair Sara Attleson, Vice Chair Cam Crawford, Secretary Brenda Hoskie and Treasurer Julie Rochman) are serving terms that end in 2027.

The Republican Party of New Mexico holds its officer elections in December, right after the general election. Democrats follow a different calendar. DPNM rules require a Spring State Central Committee (SCC) meeting and officer elections in odd-numbered years (DPNM State Rules, Article II, Rule 1.3). The process also starts at the grassroots level, with county party reorganization meetings that choose the State Central Committee members who will cast the votes.

Important: As of this writing, DPNM has not published its 2027 filing deadline, candidacy form or meeting date. The party’s “Run for State Party Office” page still shows the 2025 races. Anyone thinking about running should watch that page and the party’s official “Call” for the spring 2027 meeting.

Run for State Party Office: https://www.nmdemocrats.org/run-for-state-party-officeLocal and county party information: https://www.nmdemocrats.org/local-party-infoCoctact 

DPNM: https://www.nmdemocrats.org/new-page

The offices on the ballot

According to party guides based on DPNM rules, the State Central Committee elects:

State ChairV

Vice Chair (At-Large

Congressional District Vice Chairs: two per congressional district, of different genders

Secretary

Treasurer 

The SCC also elects New Mexico’s members of the Democratic National Committee (DNC) and members of several party committees, including SPARC, the Affirmative Action Committee and the Budget & Finance Committee.

In 2025, DPNM handled these races in two parts. One online form was for candidates declaring for chair, vice chair, secretary and treasurer. A separate sign-up was for candidates for CD vice chair or committee seats.

How to run: step by step

Read the rules and the job descriptions. DPNM’s run-for-office page links to the roles and responsibilities of each position, drawn from the party rules. The party itself notes that much of an officer’s work goes beyond what the rules list.

Watch for the 2027 Call and filing window. The Spring SCC meeting is announced through an official Call from the state chair. In 2025, candidates declared online through the party’s run-for-office page.

Declare your candidacy using the form DPNM posts for the 2027 cycle. Use the separate CD vice chair and committee sign-up if that is the seat you want.

Campaign to State Central Committee members. As with the Republican Party, rank-and-file voters do not elect state party officers. SCC members do.

Get your county party’s help, or become an SCC member yourself (see below).

Who votes: the State Central Committee

The State Central Committee is the governing body of the Democratic Party of New Mexico and oversees its political affairs. It has roughly 500 members, most of them volunteers elected at the county level.

How seats are assigned: Seats are apportioned to each county based on Democratic voter turnout. Members are elected at-large within each county.

Tribal seats: In 2023, DPNM added 14 SCC positions set aside for members of sovereign tribal nations (Article II, Rule 1.2.8).

Meetings: The SCC meets at least twice a year.

How SCC members are chosen: In odd-numbered years, county parties reorganize. Ward meetings elect members of the County Central Committee. The County Central Committee then elects the county chair, vice chair(s) and the county’s State Central Committee members. In 2023, those county meetings had to be held between March 8 and April 1, before the April state meeting. Bernalillo County alone elects 162 SCC members, 129 in CD 1 and 33 in CD 2.

That means a New Mexico Democrat who wants a voice in choosing the state chair can start by running for ward, county or SCC positions at their county party’s spring meeting.

How the vote works

Unlike the Republican Party’s in-person floor vote, DPNM conducts officer elections by absentee ballot, and all SCC votes are non-secret ballots (DPNM Rules, Article I, Rule 5.6). Proxies can be used for in-person votes but not for absentee ballots.

In 2025, SCC members voted by secure online absentee ballot from April 19 to April 26. Results were announced at the spring SCC meeting at the Albuquerque Little Theater. A total of 466 SCC members, about 97%, voted.

Officers serve two-year terms.

What each officer does, and why it matters

A state party runs the organization behind its candidates: it recruits volunteers, registers voters, raises money, coordinates campaigns, writes the platform, and fills ballot vacancies when needed. In 2026, for example, DPNM’s State Central Committee chose the party’s lieutenant governor nominee after the primary winner withdrew.

State Chair

The chair is the chief executive of DPNM. The chair manages party affairs and election campaigns and must stay neutral in Democratic primaries. The chair also:

Appoints all members of the State Rules Committee, some members of the other standing committees, and any additional committeesServes on the Democratic National CommitteeNominates presidential electors

Why it matters: The chair sets the party’s strategy, oversees its staff and budget, and is the main public voice of New Mexico Democrats going into the 2028 cycle.

Vice Chair (At-Large)

The vice chair serves on the DNC, chairs the party’s Judicial Council, and must stay neutral in Democratic primaries.

Why it matters: The vice chair gives New Mexico a second seat on the national party’s governing body and leads the internal panel that hears party disputes.

Congressional District Vice Chairs

Each of New Mexico’s three congressional districts elects two vice chairs, of different genders, through the SCC.

Why it matters: These officers give each region, from the Albuquerque metro to southern New Mexico to the north and tribal lands, a voice in state party leadership.

Secretary

The secretary is elected by the SCC and handles the party’s official records.

Why it matters: Accurate records, notices and minutes are what make party votes and actions valid.

Treasurer

The treasurer chairs the Budget & Finance Committee and must stay neutral in Democratic primaries.

Why it matters: The treasurer oversees the party’s money and its legal compliance.

Leadership can come from the grassroots level.

item.title: Alamogordo Native's 'The Cosmic Trigger: Trinity 1945' Earns Five International Festival Honors
item.description:
SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. / ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Eighty-one years after the world's first atomic bomb lit up the desert sky about 60 miles northwest of Alamogordo, a filmmaker who grew up on New York Avenue is taking the story of what came next to international audiences.

The Cosmic Trigger: Trinity 1945, the feature-length historical documentary co-directed by Larry L. Sheffield and Trent J. Di Giulio, has won five international film festival awards in the United States and Europe since its 2026 theatrical release. The 75-minute film looks into the reports of unexplained aerial phenomena over southern New Mexico in the years after the July 16, 1945, Trinity test.

It is the final film in Sheffield's atomic-era trilogy, following Oppenheimer After Trinity (2023) and The Atomic Rocketeer(2024). Its honors so far:

World Film Festival in Cannes (May 2026) — Best Historical Film

Oniros Film Awards, New York (May 2026) — Best Historical Film

Cine Paris Film Festival (May 2026) — Best War Theme Film

RED Movie Awards, Reims (2026 seasonal) — Best Documentary (Feature)

ICE Movie Awards, Courchevel (2026 seasonal) — Best Documentary (Feature); finalist for the annual Grand Finale

The film was also an Official Selection of the 2026 Coronado Island Film Festival, where it screened at the Village Theatre in November.

The film's road to Cannes ran through downtown Alamogordo. The Cosmic Trigger had its world premiere at the Oppenheimer Festival in Los Alamos in August 2025 and its Alamogordo premiere on May 16, 2026, at the Flickinger Center for the Performing Arts on New York Avenue. The Flickinger had already hosted the local premieres of Sheffield's earlier films: Oppenheimer After Trinity in May 2023 and The Atomic Rocketeer in May 2024. The new film then ran Sept. 11–17 at the Harkins Shea 14 in Scottsdale, where Sheffield now lives.

Sheffield's production company, First Light Productions, is based in the Phoenix area, but his roots are in the Tularosa Basin. His father, Leonard Sheffield, came to Alamogordo for a summer job in 1953 and moved back for good in 1957 to manage Stevenson's Hardware and Furniture at 919 New York Ave. He later became its majority owner, brought a Montgomery Ward store to 822 New York Ave., and opened Sheffield's Furniture and Carpet on White Sands Boulevard. Leonard Sheffield also served eight terms in the New Mexico Legislature and kept close ties with Holloman Air Force Base.

To mark the May premiere, the Sheffield family announced a gift to the city: a historic street clock reading "Est. 1898," with "Alamogordo" in gold lettering, to stand near 822 New York Ave.

The trilogy began with a family mystery. Sheffield's grandfather held a classified clearance and worked on the Manhattan Project, moving between Oak Ridge, Tenn., Hanford, Wash., and Los Alamos over about two years. He never talked about the work. Sheffield learned about it only after his grandfather died, and in 2019 he began the research that turned into four films.

The first, the short Alamogordo, Center of the World: Trinity 1945, explained why the area around Alamogordo was picked for the first nuclear test. According to Alamogordo Town News, Sheffield's films together had earned more than 33 national and international festival awards before this year's run.

For Otero County, the Trinity story is local history. The test took place at 5:29 a.m. on part of the Alamogordo Bombing and Gunnery Range, northwest of what was then Alamogordo Army Air Field. To keep the test secret, the airfield put out a press release blaming the flash on an accidental explosion at an ammunition dump. The truth came out only after Hiroshima was bombed on Aug. 6.

The airfield, six miles west of town, opened in 1942 and trained crews flying B-17, B-24 and B-29 bombers. After the war it became a center for testing guided missiles and pilotless aircraft, and on Jan. 13, 1948, it was renamed Holloman Air Force Base. White Sands Proving Ground was formally set up on July 9, 1945, just a week before Trinity. (The bases and testing grounds named in the film sometimes appear under their later names. In the summer of 1945, "Holloman" was still Alamogordo Army Air Field.)

The Cosmic Trigger is set in that period of rapid military growth around Alamogordo, from 1945 through 1957. Rather than relying on folklore, the filmmakers say, the documentary is built on newly found declassified military records, archival footage and firsthand accounts from engineers, scientists and service members stationed near Los Alamos, White Sands Proving Ground and the Alamogordo airfield.

"This isn't about myths or folklore," Sheffield said in announcing the film. He calls it a close look at documented events in the skies over what he describes as America's atomic frontier. Viewers will draw their own conclusions about what the witnesses saw. The film's value for local audiences may lie as much in its archival record of the Tularosa Basin in those years as in any single answer.

The film's success comes as the Tularosa Basin is still dealing with Trinity's human cost. Local residents were not warned or evacuated before the 1945 blast. In July 2025, Congress expanded the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act (RECA) to cover New Mexico "downwinders" for the first time, after a campaign of about 20 years led by the Tularosa Basin Downwinders Consortium and co-founder Tina Cordova.

People who lived in New Mexico for at least one year between 1944 and late 1962 and developed one of the covered cancers may qualify for a one-time payment of $100,000, and family members can file for a relative who has died. The deadline to file is Dec. 31, 2027. Source NM reported in July that more than $55 million had been paid to New Mexicans since the expansion. State officials have warned residents about firms charging fees to file claims that can be filed for free.

After its run of awards in Europe and New York, The Cosmic Trigger is still on the festival circuit, including its standing as a finalist for the ICE Movie Awards' annual Grand Finale. For Alamogordo audiences, the film adds a new chapter to a story that began in their own backyard, told by someone who grew up there.

Sources: Alamogordo Town News / 2nd Life Media; Mesilla Valley Film Society; Holloman AFB 704th/96th Test Group history; Holloman AFB, "Atomic Age: Alamogordo and the Bomb"; KRWG; Source NM; Paradise Valley Independent; Flickinger Center.

item.title: In Memory of Randy Lee Burrows
item.description:
Randy Lee Burrows of Alamogordo, New Mexico passed away on November 15th, 2026 at the age of 73. He was born on October 22 1953 in Wallace, Idaho, to Elvin Elmer Sherman and Theo Holly (Strub) Burrows. Most of his childhood was spent in Belgrade, Montana until he enlisted in the United States Air Force in 1974 where he served our country for the next 20 years. His career in the USAF would send him to Louisiana where he would meet and marry the love of his life, Susan (Daw) Burrows, and together they would spend the next 30 years traveling and raising their daughter, Stacey.

After retirement from the Air Force, he drove for Swift trucking for 6 years and enjoyed working at Dave’s Guns, the Sydney Paul Gordon Shooting Range, and O’Reilly’s before entering a well-earned full retirement

He counted his fellowship with the Tularosa Masonic Lodge No. 49 and the Alamogordo chapter of the Widows Sons Masonic Riders Association among the most important times of his life, wearing his membership in both organizations with great pride.

Randy is survived by his daughter, Stacey Loose, son-in-law, Bill Loose, and adored grandson, Michael Loose all of Alamogordo. In addition he is survived by his mother, Holly; brothers and sisters-in-law, Allen and Julie Burrows and Tony and Patty Burrows; his sister and brother-in-law, Lori and Dan Love; his sister, Janine Burrows; his sister-in-law, Bertha Vallery; his honorary brother, Fred Martin; numerous cherished nieces and nephews; and his spoiled but treasured dog, Sadie Mae, who has been his faithful companion for over 12 years. He leaves behind a circle of deeply devoted friends who made it their mission to care for and support him whenever he was in need.

He was preceded in death by his loving wife, Susan; his beloved in-laws, William and Sybil Daw; his adopted father, Forrest Burrows; and his father, Elvin Elmer Sherman.

Randy enjoyed sharing his musical talents, looked for any excuse to travel and experience new adventures especially by motorcycle, and was always known to talk about how proud he was of his family.

The family has entrusted his remains to the Scenic Chapel for care and cremation.

Should you wish to make a memorial contribution, the family kindly suggests donations to the Gary Sinise Foundation to support of veterans, their families, and first responders or to a charity of your choice.

item.title: County Shooting Range Draws 227 Competitors From 14 States as Championship Match Returns
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Otero County’s Sidney Paul Gordon Shooting Range hosted 227 competitors from 14 states in October for the 2026 New Mexico High Desert Championship Match, a turnout nearly 60 percent larger than the first time the range held the event two years ago.

The figures come from the October 2026 range report that Range Master Mark Douglas prepared Nov. 9 for the Otero County manager and county commissioners. The report says the 2024 match drew 143 participants. This year 270 people registered and 227 attended.

New Mexico supplied the largest group of shooters at 132, followed by Arizona with 47, Texas with 22 and Colorado with 14. Oklahoma and California sent two each, and one competitor apiece came from Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Florida, Idaho, Minnesota and Missouri.

227 competitors. 14 states. Every bay on the range in use.

Douglas credited match coordinator Jeremy Kirschbaum with driving the growth, writing that Kirschbaum and his team built challenging stages that renewed interest in the event.

The match was large enough to take over the entire facility. Stage construction began five days before competitors arrived, with the local club, the Otero Practical Shooters Association, starting setup on a Monday. The Picacho Gun Club of Las Cruces brought materials for four stages, and clubs from as far as Albuquerque supplied the remaining five, according to the report.

A part-time range safety officer identified in the report as Jeff stayed on site in his RV as camp host, which let the gates open at 6 a.m. He also brought his own tractor to groom bays and spread gravel after heavy rain damaged the grounds the week before.

HOP Munitions of Perrysville, Ohio, sponsored the match with 15,000 rounds of 9mm ammunition, and its operations manager, Tyler Flinn, flew in to attend.

Douglas wrote that the county’s acquisition of 45 adjacent acres should eventually let the range host large events while keeping several bays open to the public.

Back-to-back late monsoon storms at the end of September and start of October left the entrance to the 400-yard bay impassable for about two days. Douglas noted that before that bay was extended and its parking area enlarged, shooting tables on the far left side would have been underwater.

The report also thanks the county Road Department for moving two shipping containers. An older 40-foot container now sits near the front gate, where it will be painted to welcome visitors. A newer 20-foot container was placed beside the range’s new 100-yard archery bay.

A week after the championship, the range held its first NRA Women on Target rifle clinic with 15 participants. Staff added the class after noticing growing interest in rifles among women attending earlier pistol clinics, and the report says the range plans to offer it again. Chuck Sampson was lead instructor, assisted by Ben Rose, with NRA Training Counselor Chelsie Zimmerman providing oversight. Bill Herndon of the Pisagah Longrifles Association gave a presentation on the history of black powder rifles.

Range staff also took part in the second annual National Night Out at the county fairgrounds, promoting firearm safety and storage. A Refuse to Be a Victim personal safety seminar drew 10 participants.

The range served 1,499 people in October, including 203 who took part in club competitions and events. It reported $8,400.48 in income against $3,668.57 in expenditures. Range fees brought in $3,427.97 and passes $2,611, with the balance from target and snack sales, donations and taxes collected.

Of the 47 passes sold, 32 went to military discount buyers, a reflection of the range’s ties to Holloman Air Force Base. The report lists local, state and federal law enforcement agencies that train at the facility, among them Alamogordo police, the Otero County Sheriff’s Office, New Mexico State Police and the U.S. Border Patrol.

item.title: Sunspot demolition to cost $26 million
item.description:
The National Science Foundation estimates that it will cost about $26 million to demolish Sunspot Solar Observatory’s smaller telescope buildings plus offices, housing and other structures, according to the NSF Fiscal Year 2026 Financial Report, released on Nov. 13. NSF also continues to claim that the site must be demolished because of a mercury leak that affects only one building.

NSF’s budget summary shows it ended the year with an unobligated balance of almost $1.9 billion, of which $1.4 billion is in Research and Related Activities, NSF’s primary funding account.

As covered in earlier ATN stories, the landmark Dunn Solar Telescope released about 186 pounds (6 quarts) of liquid, elemental mercury from a large bearing that let the telescope’s main barrel and observing platform rotate smoothly as they observed the Sun. An engineering inspection revealed a crack in a faulty weld, apparently there since the Dunn was completed in 1969. Concerned that the leak could reopen and spill the 18,000-pound load of mercury, NSF decided to drain all the mercury and to demolish the Dunn and the rest of Sunspot.

In Note 6. Environmental and disposal liabilities (pg. 29), NSF repeats its claim that it is “demolishing Sacramento Peak Observatory, including the visitor center, due to a mercury leak from the Dunn Solar Telescope,” although it has never identified any contamination outside the Dunn. Demolition of the Dunn is scheduled to be complete by late March 2027, with the rest of Sunspot gone by Fall 2027. Sunspot Community Center and Basin Alliance are leading efforts to preserve as much of Sunspot as possible for dark sky astrotourism and other historical educational purposes.

Sunspot started in 1947 as one of the first space weather forecasting stations, with two observers and a telescope operating out of the back of a truck. It soon grew into a world-class solar science research center with the Dunn, the Evans Solar Facility, and Patrol Dome/Hilltop Lab. Because it was a remote installation — Sunspot highway was not built until the 1960s — included a village with 35 houses (only 16 remain), a VIP apartment with dormitory, and a community center. NSF took over in 1976 following a change in Federal funding.

NSF has allocated up to $20 million to demolish the Dunn. Of that, $13.7 million has been obligated to Thornton Tomasetti, an international engineering firm. As of Sept. 30 (the end of Federal fiscal year 2026), NSF estimated that demolition of the rest of Sunspot would cost another $26 million as compared to $1.5 million a year to operate, as reported in other sources.

Note 6 also reports asbestos liabilities of $45 million for all of NSF’s facilities. It has no breakdown for sites, although Sunspot has asbestos insulation, ceiling tiles, and flooring adhesives, as well as lead-based paint and plumbing, all consistent with 1950s and ‘60s construction practices. Federal law requires that these be safely removed before demolishing a building. Despite the age of those buildings, NSF reports it “does not have any deferred maintenance to report … .”

Note: The author, Dave Dooling is a veteran science writer and former education officer at the National Solar Observatory.

item.title: It’s Sangria Law for Thanksgiving 2026 in New Mexico
item.description:
Every family has rules. Ours has the Sangria Law.

It began in 2019, when our friends Chris & Gretchen showed up to Thanksgiving with a punch bowl the size of a satellite dish. Inside were red wine, brandy, orange slices, and what they called “a few apples.” We later counted fourteen. Our friend Lynn said it looked like a fruit salad that had made some poor life choices.

By the time the turkey came out, the sangria bowl was half full and our friend Martin’ was on a chair giving a toast to the dog. Uncle Fred tapped his glass and announced, “From now on, sangria is the official drink of Thanksgiving. This is law.”

Real laws need approval, though, and in our family only one body has that power: the Thanksgiving Seniors’ Table.

Grandpa at age 90, Rene, Aunt Deb, and Mr. Carson from the neighborhood who has come every year to celebrate with us and nobody remembers inviting, put down their forks and talked it over for a long time. Then Mr Carson raised his wine glass. “Approved Thanksgiving is now a day of Sangria Law,” he said, “as long as it contains the best in wines and brandy.”

That’s how the Wine Exception was written into the law.

The next year, Cousin Katie tried to bring some craft beer, while it was appreciated Uncle Dave looked at the six-pack like it had insulted his mother. “Section 2,” he said. “You’ve been warned we operate Thanksgiving under Sangria Law.”

That’s when we realized the Sangria Law had sections.

THE SANGRIA LAW

Ratified by the Seniors’ Table, 2019. Amended yearly, usually after dessert, multiple glasses shared and a nap or two. 

Section 1: The Pour. Sangria must be served before the turkey. Grace may not be said until every adult holds at least one glass with an orange slice.

Section 2: Contraband. Anyone who brings a drink that isn’t sangria has to sit next to Grandpa Bob while he shares his thoughts on Thanksgiving football. 

Section 3: The Wine Exception. Plain wine is allowed, since it’s just sangria that hasn’t gone to fruit school yet. The Seniors’ Table gets first pick of every bottle. Anyone under 65 who opens the good Cabernet without permission will be tried by the Seniors’ Table, and no ruling will come down until after a game of scrabble. 

Section 4: Fruit Rights. Fruit at the bottom of the pitcher belongs to whoever drained it. Fights over the last soggy apple go to the Pie Court.

Section 5: The Cranberry Clause. Leftover cranberry sauce may legally be added to the sangria. Nobody has done this. Everyone thinks about it.

Section 6: Spill Liability. Spill sangria or wine on the white tablecloth and you’re on dish duty detail with no appeal. (Precedent: Katie v. The Tablecloth, 2021.)

Section 7: Toasting Limits. Each guest gets three toasts. Everyone at the Seniors’ Table gets unlimited toasts under the “We’ve Earned It” exemption. Grandpa’s toasts to the dog count double.

Section 8: The Designated Driver Amendment. Drivers get the “Virgin Sangria,” which is fancy grape juice with a cinnamon stick and available to children and those who don’t partake in alcohol. They’re allowed to look smug about it.

Section 9: The Leftover Doctrine. Leftover sangria may not be poured out. It has to be drunk on Black Friday, ideally while waiting in a checkout line and questioning everything. Leftover wine goes home with the Seniors’ Table with a few bottles to the host.  That part isn’t up for debate.

These days the Sangria Law is and will remain an understood family tradition. Every year there is a toast to Sangria law, and the kids giggle at the Cranberry Clause, and the Seniors’ Table raises their wine glasses to make it official all over again.

Last year Katie’s husband asked, “Is this legally binding?”

Rene filled his glass to the brim and dropped in three orange slices. Over at the Seniors’ Table, Grandpa Bob gave a slow, serious nod.

“Son,” Rene said, “in this house, it’s the only thing that’s binding.”

Happy Thanksgiving. Pour responsibly, and obey the Law. 🍷🦃

Disclosure by Journalist Chris Edwards:

“Sangria Law” is a play on words, part of a long line of internet puns on “Sharia law” that also includes “Shakira law” and “Shawarma law.” The joke is aimed at fearmongering, not at any faith or the people who practice it. Satire has always been one of a free society’s best answers to hate, and this story is offered in that spirit.

It’s also constitutionally sound(ish). The First Amendment protects freedom of speech and freedom of religion, and the Twenty-First Amendment ended Prohibition and left each state to set its own alcohol rules. Sangria Law is enforced only at our dinner table, only by the Seniors’ Table, and only on people who bring craft beer.

item.title: Animal Village NM Takes Spay/Neuter Registration Online, Cuts Copays
item.description:
OTERO COUNTY, N.M. — Animal Village NM has moved registration for its low-cost spay and neuter program online, a change the nonprofit says will let pet owners in Otero and Lincoln counties sign up without missing work or burning gas on long drives.

The group's first virtual registration was "a huge success," according to an organization spokesperson. Starting Jan. 27, online registration sessions will be held monthly. Pet owners can pre-qualify and find details at animalvillagenm.com.

Through a partnership with Paw and Hand Veterinary Care, Animal Village NM has lowered its copays to $35 for cats and $65 for dogs. The price covers the surgery, a rabies vaccine, a microchip, pain medication and a post-surgical recovery bag.

Animal Village NM is seeking dependable volunteers and monthly donors. Gifts of $10 or $25 a month help the group plan ahead, it said, so staff can spend less time worrying about funding, supplies and volunteer shortages and more time helping local pets.

Since 2007, Animal Village NM has provided more than 11,000 spay and neuter surgeries.

To register for assistance, volunteer or donate, visit animalvillagenm.com.

item.title: New Mexico GOP's failed court fight over chair leaves questions about legal costs
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — The Republican Party of New Mexico fought in court this spring to keep Amy Barela as its chair and lost. Months later, the cost of that fight and who paid for it have not been publicly reported. A few GOP insiders from Northern New Mexico are pouring over the state financial filings and asking questions. 

The dispute began when Barela ran for re-election to the Otero County Commission while leading the state party. Party rules call for a state officer to surrender the party post when another Republican is in the same race. Barela maintained the rule did not cover her because she filed before her opponent, Jonathan Emery. A parliamentarian the party hired agreed with her, the Santa Fe New Mexican reported.

Emery and two statewide candidates, Duke Rodriguez and Aubrey Blair Dunn, sued on April 30, according to judicial records. 

On May 27, Judge Cindy Mercer issued a preliminary injunction barring Barela from continuing as chair. The order also barred Barela and two other party officials from publicly backing one Republican over another in contested primaries. A preliminary injunction is not a final ruling in the case.

The party appealed. Its petition argued that courts should not settle internal party disputes and that the order violated members' free speech rights. The state Supreme Court unanimously denied the petition June 10 without explanation, per court records.

Barela lost her primary to Emery on June 2.

Attorney Carter Harrison argued the party's case.

The Albuquerque Journal described him as also representing Barela and other top party officials.

Lawyers commonly represent an organization and its officers in the same case, and professional rules permit it when each client consents. Nothing in the public record indicates the arrangement was improper but the question is why were political dollars that might have helped fund winning campaigns used for lawsuits in the first place, rather then the chair just step down and the endorsements be pulled with a simple party leadership apology. 

What the record does not show is who the firm's clients were, which account paid the bills, how much was spent, and whether and who within  a party committee approved the expense.

It also does not show who consented on the party's behalf to sharing an attorney with its chair, or whether any individual defendant paid a share. Those questions are not accusations of wrongdoing doing they are questions of transparency, accountability and process. Questions rank and file Republicans who contribute to the party should be asking. 

The party's campaign finance reports are public, and itemized payments in those filings would show any fees paid to the firm. The party leadership owes answers to the SCC and the public at large. As such it’s hoped that this becomes an agenda item at the January SCC meeting for a response and that those seeking Party leadership roles respond to those questions.

item.title: Timberon Water District Faces New Billing Complaint as PRC Receivership Consideration Deadline Nears
item.description:
TIMBERON, N.M. — Two Timberon residents have asked state regulators to open a district-wide investigation into missed meter readings and unissued water bills at the Timberon Water and Sanitation District (TWSD), adding to the pressure on a district that has until Dec. 7 to tell the New Mexico Public Regulation Commission why it should not be fined, put under court order, or handed to a receiver.

The new complaint, filed late Sunday, arrives as the New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) confirms the district remains out of compliance with drinking-water rules over deficiencies identified in 2025 — and as a public records request this newspaper filed in August remains unfulfilled.

Mark Harding and Barbara Shockley, residential TWSD customers representing themselves, filed a joint formal complaint and request for a district-wide investigation with the PRC. The filing was stamped Nov. 22 at 4:38 p.m. under Docket No. 26-0000202; the document itself is dated Nov. 23.

According to the complaint:

https://drive.google.com/file/d/1MPQ2h3lkq0yzxxIUUbq9g8LAkl-AWw5E/view?usp=drivesdk

On Sept. 10, the couple photographed their meter showing a reading higher than the one later listed for Sept. 18 on their September bill.

They filed an informal complaint with the PRC on Nov. 2 about delayed readings, missing bills and the September discrepancy. The PRC acknowledged it Nov. 5, and on Nov. 17 commission staff indicated TWSD had not yet responded.

A TWSD employee read their meter on Nov. 18. As of Nov. 21, they say they had received neither an October nor a November bill.

The district's agenda for a Nov. 23 special board meeting stated that October 2026 bills had not been issued and overlap the November billing cycle, and proposed discussing separate or combined statements and new due dates.

The complainants warn that combining two or more billing periods could hit some households with balances of $400 to $500 or more — figures they describe as illustrative, not actual bills — and could fall hardest on low- and fixed-income customers. They also argue delayed billing may squeeze the district's own cash flow and ask TWSD to disclose how many accounts and how much revenue are affected.

The complaint points to a possible technical cause. At its Nov. 10 meeting, district management reportedly discussed needing programming work to move electronic meter readings into its UBMax billing software, for which vendor support reportedly ended in October 2024. The complainants stress that neither the support status nor any link to billing errors has been independently established.

Harding emailed General Manager and records custodian Wendy Case an Inspection of Public Records Act (IPRA) request on Nov. 12 seeking UBMax licensing, support, payment and data-integrity records. As of Nov. 21, he reports no acknowledgment or production.

Harding and Shockley ask the commission to require a verified written response from TWSD; reconcile original meter readings, reader exports and account ledgers; correct verified discrepancies with credits or refunds; protect customers from late fees, collections or shutoffs caused solely by district billing delays; preserve billing records back to June 2024; and order a corrective-action plan with firm deadlines for restoring monthly billing.

The filing also notes that Harding's earlier PRC complaint, Case 25-00011-UT, was closed by a commission order dated Nov. 20, 2026, and that the pair has moved to intervene in the commission's show-cause case against the district.

That show-cause case, Docket No. 26-0000191, was opened on the commission's own motion. The order, signed Nov. 5 and filed Nov. 6 by Commissioners Gabriel Aguilera, Greg Nibert and Patrick J. O'Connell, directs TWSD to explain why it should not face monetary penalties, an injunction or writ of mandamus, or appointment of a receiver.

The order cites four areas of alleged violation: failure to maintain facilities for continuous, adequate water service; inadequate water pressure; a $30-a-year "Facilities and Services Fee" charged since 2012 without PRC approval; and failure to file annual reports for 2024 and 2025.

Commissioners also directed PRC Public Interest Advocacy Staff to investigate whether TWSD carried out the financial, accounting and engineering plans it filed in its 2023 rate case, and how it spent the additional revenue from the higher rates approved there. Factual claims in the district's response must be backed by sworn affidavit. The commission has not yet decided whether to hold a public hearing.

Key dates in the case:

Dec. 7, 2026 — TWSD's response due

Dec. 18, 2026 — PRC staff preliminary investigation report due

Jan. 4, 2027 — deadline for customers and other interested parties to move to intervene

Jan. 6, 2027 — replies from staff and interested parties due

"I think that the PRC is going to put TWSD in receivership in the next couple months," said an individual with close ties to the system. The commission has not made any such determination, and receivership is one of several remedies listed in the order.

In a written statement to Alamogordo Town News, NMED spokesperson Jorge Armando Estrada laid out the district's recent violations:

March 5, 2026: NMED issued a Notice of Violation under the federal Ground Water Rule for failing to correct significant deficiencies identified during the 2025 sanitary survey.

June 9, 2026: NMED issued a second notice for failing to give customers public notice of the March violation. TWSD issued that notice July 30, returning to compliance on the notification requirement. "However, the system remains out of compliance for failure to correct the significant deficiencies," Estrada wrote.

Aug. 10, 2026: NMED cited the district for missing the deadline to notify customers of a June 16, 2025, operator-certification violation. Notice was due June 16, 2026, but went out July 30. The underlying operator violation was resolved when TWSD contracted Level 4 operator Alex Salas on July 17, 2025.

NMED also issued TWSD an Administrative Compliance Order on Aug. 1, 2025, and is "currently engaged in settlement negotiations," Estrada said.

Previous reporting found that order assessed $62,620 in civil penalties, which the district appealed.

NMED's enforcement documents for Timberon are posted at env.nm.gov/enforcement-watch.

On Nov. 13, Alamogordo Town News asked Case for an update on an IPRA request submitted in August that has not been fulfilled. Case replied the same day that she had forwarded the request "to John," adding that he "is now taking care of all IPRA request." The email did not give his full name or title, and the district has not announced a new records custodian.

After 11 days with no further word, Alamogordo Town News again wrote to Case on Nov. 24, asking her to identify John and provide a status update on the request. Case had not responded by press time.

Under IPRA, a records custodian must allow inspection promptly and no later than 15 days after receiving a written request, or notify the requester within that window if the request is excessively burdensome and more time is needed.

The district's prior records custodian, Leo McAtee, left TWSD in late July after a series of negative emails and statement to Alamogordo Town News. 

TWSD's sworn response in the show-cause case is due Dec. 7, followed by the PRC staff report Dec. 18. The commission has not yet acted on the Harding–Shockley complaint. TWSD did not respond to a request for comment by press time. 

Disclosure: 2nd Life Media Alamogordo Town News and editor Chris Edwards are parties to records disputes with TWSD described in this article.
