item.title: Construction Visible at Rad Retrocade and Sands Theater After Rardin Questions LEDA Spending
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO — In late October, Mayor Pro-Tem Joshua Rardin questioned where $2 million in city economic development money had gone. All the while new stucco, a new sign and fresh concrete are showing up at the two New York Avenue businesses that received it.

Rardin's remarks are now part of the official record and look poorly on an ill informed commissioner. The minutes of the October 27 City Commission meeting were in the agenda packet for the November 17 regular meeting, where they came up for approval on the consent agenda.

According to the approved minutes, Rardin used the "Remarks and Inquiries" part of the October 27 meeting to talk about Local Economic Development Act (LEDA) projects on New York Avenue. He noted that this was a recurring topic.

The minutes summarize his point this way: LEDA funds are typically approved and then paid out as businesses submit invoices. For two downtown projects, however, $1,000,000 checks were cut up front to each business owner "without current recourse or tracking of how funds were expended." This statement is untrue the terms of the agreement require an annual update from the business owners. 

Rardin asked the city's auditors to look closely at the New York Avenue LEDA funds in the latest fiscal year's financial records during the upcoming audit, "to safeguard taxpayer money."

The minutes don't name the two projects. The city's two $1 million downtown LEDA awards went to Rad Retrocade in the 800 block and the White Sands Theater in the 1000 block. The commission approved the Rad Retrocade award 7-0 in May 2025.

Rardin wasn't the only one to talk about the downtown projects that night. During public comment, resident Beth Crabbe called statements about the projects' status at the previous commission meeting "erroneous, irresponsible," and said they misrepresented public facts, according to the minutes. She criticized what she described as past displays of unfairness by Rardin. She also urged the city manager to get proper factual data before making public statements about downtown projects.

Both business owners have told Alamogordo Town News that their projects are moving forward and that they are complying with their city agreements. They say they have submitted receipts and status updates, and each plans to put more than $1 million of their own money into their building. The city's first formal LEDA check-in under the contracts is due at the end of December.

Anyone walking the 800 block of New York Avenue this month can see that Rad Retrocade is moving forward. A new illuminated sign now hangs on the building's brick front: "RAD" in hot-pink script with a teal outline over the word "RETROCADE."

Through the storefront windows you can see a lot of interior work. New concrete has been poured, and plumbing and other building infrastructure are being installed. That's the kind of groundwork a restaurant, bar and arcade needs before it can open its doors.

Rad Retrocade already runs a location in Las Cruces. When the Alamogordo project was approved, it was pitched as a family-friendly, retro-themed arcade with a restaurant and bar, meant to bring evening foot traffic downtown.

A few blocks north, the historic Sands Theater, which opened as the White Sands Theatre in 1937, is clearly an active construction site.

The long side wall facing the neighboring gravel lot has a fresh coat of gray stucco from end to end. Old openings in the wall have been patched, and some areas still show the black weather barrier underneath. Along the base of the wall sit a large mixing tub, stacks of mortar buckets, bags of material, troweling tools and a line of safety cones, along with rebar pins and new concrete forms.

Out front, the same gray base coat now covers part of the theater's old teal facade beside the entrance. The classic red, yellow and blue marquee still hangs over the sidewalk. Inside, crews are working throughout the building, including in the theater room itself.

Owner Troy Stegner has said the restoration will bring back the building's Art Deco character while updating the interior for events such as esports tournaments, watch parties and independent film screenings.

Both businesses are getting ready to relaunch in 2027. Downtown leaders see them as anchors for the next phase of the New York Avenue revival, which follows the city and Alamogordo MainStreet's completed makeover of the 800 and 900 blocks.

The LEDA spending question will come back in front of the public soon. The first formal check-in under the contracts is due at the end of December, and the city's next audit will cover the fiscal year in question. For now, on New York Avenue, the work is visible from the sidewalk.

The Alamogordo City Commission's November 17, 2026 agenda packet, including the October 27 minutes, is available on the city website at ci.alamogordo.nm.us.

item.title: Lawsuit says Otero County jail ignored inmate's meningitis symptoms before his death
item.description:
Alamogordo NM- A wrongful death lawsuit has been filed on behalf of an inmate who died more than two years ago while in the custody of the Otero County Detention Center. It is the latest in a series of legal challenges over how the Alamogordo jail and its contracted medical provider care for the people held there.

Tracy Graham, the personal representative of Robert Joseph Gutierrez Jr.'s estate, filed the lawsuit in September in 12th Judicial District Court. It names the Otero County Commission, the Otero County Detention Center and VitalCore Health Strategies, the company contracted to provide medical care to inmates at the jail.

The lawsuit alleges that staff ignored signs that Gutierrez had meningitis, and that this neglect led to his death in September 2024. Graham is seeking compensatory damages for Gutierrez's pain and suffering, plus his medical, hospital and funeral costs.

Weeks of symptoms, then a fall

According to the lawsuit, Gutierrez complained in the weeks before his death that he was "not feeling well." He also had headaches and a fever.

His cellmate saw him fall on Sept. 9, 2024. Jail officers found him on the floor of his cell at about 1 a.m. the next day, the lawsuit says.

He was taken to the emergency room at a local hospital, where he had a seizure, the lawsuit states. A CT scan showed a "juxta ventricular enhancing lesion" in his left frontal lobe, among other "concerning findings."

Because his condition was so severe, Gutierrez was airlifted to University Medical Center in El Paso, Texas. He had another seizure on the way, and tests showed a "severe brain injury," according to the lawsuit.

By Sept. 14, 2024, Gutierrez was "unresponsive, his pupils were fixed and dilated, and he had no spontaneous movements, cough, or gag reflexes," the lawsuit states. He was pronounced dead later that day.

The County of El Paso Office of the Medical Examiner ruled that his cause of death was acute meningitis. Hypertensive cardiovascular disease was listed as a contributing factor.

"The Defendant's failure to recognize the obvious signs of a serious medical condition and its failure to provide timely and adequate medical care constituted a breach of its duty to Mr. Gutierrez," the lawsuit states. "This breach directly and proximately caused his untreated meningitis to progress, leading to his immense pain and suffering and ultimately his wrongful death."

A medical emergency

Meningitis is swelling of the lining of the brain and spinal cord. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention lists fever, headache and a stiff neck as its common symptoms, and calls bacterial meningitis a medical emergency that should be treated as soon as possible. The CDC says death from bacterial meningitis can come within a few hours, though most people recover if they are treated properly. Later symptoms can include seizures and coma.

The lawsuit does not say what caused Gutierrez's meningitis.

The defendants respond

A lawyer for VitalCore filed a response to the lawsuit. For each allegation, the company either denied it or said it didn't have enough information to respond.

Representatives from Otero County did not respond to a request for comment. The county's attorney has declined to comment on pending lawsuits in the past.

VitalCore is based in Topeka, Kansas. According to The Gazette in Colorado Springs, it was founded in January 2015 as Viola Riggin LLC and took the VitalCore name in 2018. The company provides health care at jails and prisons in several states, and it has faced wrongful death lawsuits elsewhere in New Mexico, including one over the death of Juan Archuleta at the Rio Arriba County jail. In August, the family of a Mississippi prisoner who died of breast cancer settled a lawsuit with VitalCore.

Concerns about jail health care raised in 2024

Questions about medical care at the Otero County jail came up months before Gutierrez died.

In 2024, 2nd Life Media's Alamogordo Town News began investigating the jail after current and former staff and detainees raised concerns about staffing, inmate care and suicides. In May 2024, the outlet reported that police and firefighters from several agencies were called to restore order after unrest at the jail on May 21.

In response to a public records request, the jail told the outlet how many medical staff were on duty. During the day there were four: two nurses or paramedics, plus a health services administrator and a director of nursing, both registered nurses. At night there were two nurses or paramedics. A mental health coordinator and a counselor worked on site during the day and were on call at other times.

In August 2024, about a month before Gutierrez died, the outlet reported that health care at the jail "remains a concern." It reported that health care staff admitted they had limited ability and capacity to give many detainees the care they needed. A former medical provider told the outlet that nurses handing out medication were supposed to have two officers with them for safety, but often had one or none.

That same August story focused on David Tomsik, who died by suicide at the jail in May 2023, according to his mother, Jena Matise. The jail reported one confirmed suicide in 2024 up to that point, a hanging in March.

$2 million paid over an earlier death

The Gutierrez lawsuit is not the first time a death at the Otero County jail has led to a lawsuit against the county and VitalCore.

Jacob Gutierrez, 26, was booked into the jail on domestic violence charges on June 9, 2023. Nine days later, he hanged himself with a phone cord, KRQE reported. He is not known to be related to Robert Gutierrez.

The New Mexico Prison & Jail Project, a nonprofit, represented Jacob Gutierrez's mother. She sued the county commission, VitalCore and several jail staff members in federal court in June 2024. Steven Robert Allen, of the nonprofit, said Jacob Gutierrez had tried to take his own life several times at the jail. Allen said that instead of getting him mental health care, staff put him alone in a cell with a phone cord. "The jail knew Jacob was suicidal," Mallory Gagan, another attorney at the nonprofit, said in a news release when the suit was filed.

The county agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle the case, and VitalCore agreed to pay another $960,000, Allen told the Santa Fe New Mexican.

According to county records reported by The Appeal, Jacob Gutierrez was one of four people who died at the jail in 2023: two by hanging, one from an overdose and one from a "medical condition."

Another lawsuit filed this spring

In April, Ann Marie Culp filed a federal civil rights lawsuit on behalf of Naomi Laycock. The suit says Laycock arrived at the jail in June 2025 with a documented history of schizophrenia and more than 10 suicide attempts. It alleges that she was cleared from close observation, that welfare checks sometimes went almost four hours apart, and that she suffered permanent brain damage after trying to hang herself with a towel. That suit names the county commission, former jail director Nena Sisler, a detention officer, a VitalCore behavioral health provider and VitalCore itself. The allegations have not been proven in court.

Staffing strains

The jail has struggled with staffing for years. In October 2023, Source NM reported that about 32% of detention center jobs were vacant. That month, the county agreed to pay Hudspeth County, Texas, $75 per person per day, plus any medical costs, to hold Otero County inmates when the jail was overcrowded or short-staffed.

A similar pattern in Lincoln County

Similar concerns have more recently come up at the Lincoln County Detention Center in Carrizozo. That jail is run by a private company, Corrections Services Group, whose contract faced a renewal decision in October.

In August, Alamogordo Town News reported that an inmate there had died by suicide in a cell with video monitoring. Days later, another inmate escaped and was quickly recaptured. The outlet reported that no nurse or medical staff is stationed at the jail overnight, which raised questions about how it could respond to medical emergencies. Unnamed sources in the Lincoln County Sheriff's Office alleged that jail leadership had discouraged staff from reporting operational problems and safety concerns to the sheriff.

The outlet filed a request under the New Mexico Inspection of Public Records Act. It asked for records on staffing levels at the time of the suicide, the jail's inmate count, documentation of the suicide and the pending contract renewal. A later story said requests for details about the suicide were still pending. In that story, the outlet also reported that the jail's compliance manager had been charged with criminal sexual penetration over an alleged relationship with an inmate. She has not been convicted.

In May, Warden Ross Castleton told Lincoln County commissioners that the jail was about six officers short and held about 70 detainees on average. He said the jail had installed new monitoring equipment for inmates on suicide watch.

item.title: In Memory of David Bobby Sanchez
item.description:
David Bobby Sanchez, 80, passed away on November 15, 2026, in Tularosa, New Mexico. He was born on August 1, 1946, in Duran, New Mexico to Fidel and Margarita (Lopez) Sanchez.

David dedicated 45 years of his life to his career as an auto body technician, taking great pride in his work. He was a man with a heart of gold, known for his kindness, generosity, and willingness to lend a helping hand to anyone in need. He never hesitated to put others before himself, leaving a lasting impression on everyone fortunate enough to know him.

David found joy in life's simple pleasures, especially camping, fishing, hunting, and sharing a dance with his beloved wife. Together, they faithfully served as Mayordomos for St. Francis de Paula Church and Santo Niño de Atocha, a reflection of their devotion to their faith and community.

One of the many things his family will cherish most is the countless stories he shared about his younger years. His stories brought laughter, wisdom, and a glimpse into the life he lived, creating precious memories that will be passed down for generations.

David will forever be remembered for his loving heart, his selfless spirit, and the beautiful memories he leaves behind. Although his presence will be deeply missed, the love he gave, the lessons he taught, and the stories he shared will live on in the hearts of those who loved him.

Survivors include his wife, Elena Sanchez; daughter, Rachael Sanchez; daughter, RoseAnn Ritch; son, Jessie Sanchez.

David leaves behind 8 grandchildren: Garett Ritch, Audriana Sanchez/Devin Aguirre, Robert Sanchez/Veronica Reyes, Joe Sanchez/Junior Lopez, Nadine Sanchez, Nevaeh Sanchez, Leilani Rico, Jamie Kaplan; 5 great grandchildren: Michael, Divinity, K’lani, Lilliana, Kashius.

He also is survived by 2 special cousins, Steve and Berna Sanchez; 5 sisters-in-law; 3 brothers-in-law; many nieces and nephews; 9 godchildren.

David is preceded in death by mother, Margarita Sanchez; father, Fidel Sanchez; grandchild, Cody Ritch; in-laws, Adela and Ramon Pino; sister-in-law, Alice Pino; numerous aunts and uncles.

Services for David will take place on Saturday, November 28, 2026, at St. Francis de Paula Catholic Church in Tularosa, New Mexico. Rosary will be recited at 10:00 am with Mass celebrated at 10:30 am with Father Martin Cornejo, Celebrant.

Burial will follow at Sacred Heart Catholic Cemetery in Tularosa.

Honorary Pallbearers include Abraham Pino, Ramon Pino Jr., Luis Pino, David Pino, Arthur Salazar, Nick Pino, Danny Pino, Sonny Silva, Frank Pino, Robert Sainz, Sam Sanchez, Daniel Martinez, Carl Galloupe, Speedy, Tranky Chavez.

item.title: Two Teens Wounded in Shooting at Alamogordo Sonic Drive-In Monday Night
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Two teenagers were wounded by gunfire in an incident at the Sonic Drive-In that began as a reported fight, according to the Alamogordo Police Department.

APD officers, assisted by Otero County Sheriff's Office deputies, responded to the restaurant Monday  after a report of a fight and shots fired. Inside the restaurant, officers found an 18-year-old male employee with an apparent gunshot wound to his lower right leg.

Officers were also sent to Christus Health, where a 17-year-old male was being treated for an apparent gunshot wound to his left hand. Police determined the two shootings were related.

APD's Criminal Investigations Division has taken over the case. Police have not released the names of those involved, the conditions of the two teens, what led to the fight, or whether any arrests have been made or suspects identified.

The case is filed under APD report number 26A-36170. Anyone with information is asked to contact the Alamogordo Police Department.

This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

item.title: Shaun Hinkle killed after pointing long gun at officers following road-rage call, State Police say
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — A 42-year-old Alamogordo man died Sunday evening after officers shot him outside his home. State Police say he walked out of his garage and pointed a long gun at officers. They had gone there to question him about a road-rage incident in which he was accused of pulling a gun on another driver.

The New Mexico State Police Investigations Bureau is investigating the shooting. It involved officers from the Alamogordo Police Department (APD) and a deputy from the Otero County Sheriff's Office (OCSO). State Police identified the man who died as Shaun Hinkle.

According to State Police, someone called 911 at about 5:21 p.m. on Nov. 23 to report a road-rage incident that started on North White Sands Boulevard. The caller said the driver of a pickup truck, later identified as Hinkle, had pointed a firearm at them. The caller took a photo of the truck and gave dispatchers its license plate number.

APD officers and an OCSO deputy went to the address where the truck was registered. State Police said they approached the house, identified themselves and repeatedly told Hinkle to come out with his hands up. Hinkle came out of a door in the garage area holding a long gun and pointed it at the officers. The officers and the deputy fired, hitting him.

Officers gave Hinkle medical aid at the scene. He was taken to an area hospital, where he was pronounced dead. No officers were hurt.

State Police will not identify the officers or the deputy who were involved. Questions about their duty status or any administrative action go to the Alamogordo Police Department and the Otero County Sheriff's Office.

State Police agents are working to independently piece together what led to the shooting. They are collecting evidence and interviewing people, and they will share what they find with the district attorney. State Police act only as factfinders in officer-involved shootings. The district attorney's office decides whether an officer's use of force was justified.

Third Alamogordo police shooting this year

State Police have now been called in to investigate at least three officer-involved shootings involving Alamogordo police in 2026. On January 14th, 2026, the New Mexico State Police Investigations Bureau was requested to investigate an officer-involved shooting (OIS) involving the Alamogordo Police Department. In that case, local police shot and killed a 41-year-old man they say was approaching them with a knife. He was later identified as Anthony Zane Blalock, 41. Then, on August 26, 2026, the New Mexico State Police Investigations Bureau was requested to investigate an officer involved shooting incident involving the Alamogordo Police Department.

The two agencies have been involved in a shooting together before. On Saturday, February 4, 2023, the New Mexico State Police Investigations Bureau was contacted to investigate an officer-involved shooting involving the Alamogordo Police Department (APD) and the Otero County Sheriff's Office (OCSO).

The investigation into Sunday's shooting is ongoing.

Source: New Mexico State Police, Otero County Sheriff’s Department

item.title: Alamogordo's Chris Edwards and Dr. Stephanie Hernandez Seek State Republican Party Officer Posts
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. — Two Alamogordo Republicans, journalist and broadcaster Chris Edwards and former Acting City Manager Dr. Stephanie Hernandez, have announced they will run for state officer positions with the Republican Party of New Mexico (RPNM). They are pitching themselves as a pragmatic, reform-minded slate after a year of infighting inside the party and heavy losses at the ballot box.

Edwards is running for 2nd Vice Chair. Hernandez is running for state party treasurer. Both races will be decided by the party's State Central Committee (SCC), the body of several hundred county-level Republicans that elects the state chair, vice chairs, secretary, treasurer and congressional district vice chairs to two-year terms. RPNM traditionally holds that vote at a December convention after the general election this year it’s been controversially decided to be in Clovis in January.

The announcements come at the end of one of the most turbulent years in recent memory for New Mexico Republicans.

In May, a state district judge ordered then-Chair Amy Barela out of her post. The ruling came under a party rule that requires a state officer to step down if they run for public office against another Republican. Barela then lost her own bid for re-election to the Otero County Commission. A June 20 SCC meeting in Las Cruces to pick her replacement failed to reach a quorum, and rival factions called competing meetings while lawsuits over party rules worked their way through the courts. First Vice Chair Mike Nelson has served as acting chair since.

The Nov. 3 general election brought more bad news for the party. Democrat Deb Haaland defeated Republican Gregg Hull for governor. U.S. Rep. Gabe Vasquez won a third term in the 2nd Congressional District over Republican Greg Cunningham. Democrats also unseated four Republican incumbents in the state House, giving them their largest majority in that chamber in more than 30 years.

Edwards is editor of 2nd Life Media AlamogordoTownNews.org and streams on KALHRadio.org He is known locally for hosting the Voices of Alamogordo candidate forums, including this spring's Otero County sheriff's forum, a November nonpartisan candidate forum and for covering the state GOP's leadership fight closely throughout 2026.

Edwards, who came of age politically in the Reagan era, said the party has to stop attacking its own members and outsiders and religious traditions, and stop relying on social issues and Christian fundamentalism to carry it forward. He wants the GOP to return to the everyday economic concerns that, in his view, built Ronald Reagan's "big tent" coalition with his morning in America business renewal appeal.

Edwards argues that extremist elements, both in New Mexico and nationally, have driven the party to its worst losses this century, and that this has to change. Both parties, he said, need to remember that people come first. As 2nd Vice Chair, his focus would be recruiting and developing candidates who put New Mexicans first.

His platform centers on inclusion, listening, and making room for a range of ideas that represent working families over corporate interests. His priorities include:

Second-chance employment for people re-entering the workforce

A renewed war on poverty

Education outcomes, with a focus on basic academic performance rather than what he calls irrelevant culture-war fights such as transgender sports

Family economics first as the party's core message

Hernandez is a lifelong Alamogordo resident and a lifelong active Republican. She describes herself as a conservative technocrat with deep experience in finance, education and veterans affairs, and she holds a Ph.D. in public administration.

She joined the City of Alamogordo as finance director in 2019 under then-City Manager Maggie Paluch. Hernandez says she led the department out of a period of questionable audits and weak accountability. She was later promoted to assistant city manager and served as acting city manager twice: from May to December 2023, after City Manager Brian Cesar retired, and again from September 2024, after Rick Holden resigned, through June 30, 2026. That adds up to roughly 27 to 28 months in the top job. For much of that time, she also covered the assistant city manager duties because the position was left unfilled.

During her tenure, millions of dollars in infrastructure projects moved forward to completion. Supporters credit her with bringing stability to a city manager's office that has seen at least seven leaders since 2015. In March 2026, the City Commission voted 7-0 to begin contract negotiations with her for the permanent job, but no contract was finalized. The city ultimately hired Robert Stockwell, who started July 1.

Outside City Hall, Hernandez has advocated for improvements at the Veterans Administration at the state and federal levels and for outcome-driven education initiatives.

If elected, she says she wants to dig into the state party's finances, conduct an audit of past performance, and bring more transparency to how the party supports its candidates.

SCC members from all 33 counties will vote on the full slate of state officers. Edwards and Hernandez are expected to campaign among committee members in Otero County and across southern New Mexico in the coming weeks.

item.title: Tiger Basketball Opens Season With 80-60 Win Over Carlsbad
item.description:
Alamogordo Town News · Nov 25, 2026

The Alamogordo Tigers boys basketball team opened its season in convincing fashion Tuesday night, beating Carlsbad 80-60 behind a balanced scoring attack and a strong middle of the game.

Jaedyn Hernandez led the way with 22 points. Aaron Herrera added 17, Eluciano Gonzales scored 13, Will Bynum had 10 and Jaycob Ochoa chipped in 8, giving the Tigers five players with eight points or more.

Fans had to be patient before tipoff. The junior varsity game went to a fourth overtime, pushing the varsity start from its scheduled 5 p.m. to around 6 p.m.

Once the varsity took the floor, Alamogordo grabbed the lead early and never gave it up. The Tigers led 20-16 after the first quarter, then used the second and third quarters to pull away, outscoring the Rams 39-26 over that stretch to take a 59-42 lead into the fourth.

Carlsbad never got closer down the stretch. Alamogordo won the fourth quarter 21-18 to finish with 80 points and a 20-point margin.

The Tigers (1-0) are off until December 3, when they face Farmington at the Capital City Tournament in Santa Fe.

item.title: Taos man charged with murder in shooting death of 17-year-old half-brother
item.description:
TAOS, N.M. — A 20-year-old man has been charged with second-degree murder in the fatal shooting of his 17-year-old half-brother inside a Taos apartment Sunday night, New Mexico State Police said.

Ivan Mikhailovich Lefebvre was arrested Monday, Nov. 23, after surrendering to officers who had surrounded a home in Ranchos de Taos for nearly six hours.

The Taos Police Department asked the State Police Investigations Bureau to take over the homicide investigation.

According to State Police, Lefebvre and his half-brother were in the apartment's living room on the evening of Sunday, Nov. 22, while three other people were in the bedrooms. Those three told investigators they heard a gunshot around 8 p.m. When they went into the living room, they found the teen on the floor with a gunshot wound. Lefebvre had already left the apartment.

Around 4 a.m. Monday, State Police and Taos police officers surrounded a residence in Ranchos de Taos where they believed Lefebvre was staying and ordered him to come outside. He surrendered at about 9:45 a.m. and was taken into custody.

During an interview with investigators, Lefebvre said he loaded a single live round into a revolver, pointed it at his half-brother and pulled the trigger, not thinking the gun would fire, according to State Police. He told investigators he got rid of the firearm after leaving the scene.

Lefebvre is charged with second-degree murder, tampering with evidence and aggravated assault.

The investigation is being handled by the New Mexico State Police Investigations Bureau.

item.title: New Interim Director: Shop Small, Celebrate Big: New York Avenue Gears Up for Small Business Saturday and Christmas on MainStreet
item.description:
ALAMOGORDO, N.M. – Historic New York Avenue is ready for the holidays. With a new cat café now open, three major building rehabilitation projects moving forward and a new interim executive director at the helm, Alamogordo MainStreet invites the community downtown for two signature events: Small Business Saturday on November 28 and Christmas on MainStreet on December 5.

Small Business Saturday – Saturday, November 28 [Confirm start/end times] Shops, restaurants and makers from the 800 Block to the 1200 Block of New York Avenue, along with businesses on White Sands Boulevard within the MainStreet District, will offer holiday specials and one-of-a-kind gifts. Small Business Saturday is a chance to keep holiday dollars local and support the family-owned businesses that give downtown its character.

Christmas on MainStreet – Saturday, December 5 [Confirm start/end times] Alamogordo's favorite downtown holiday tradition returns to New York Avenue with festive lights, local entertainment, food, holiday shopping and family fun. Watch Alamogordo MainStreet's social media for the full lineup, vendor information and street closures.

Also nearby: The City of Alamogordo's Christmas Tree Lighting is Friday, December 4, at Washington Park, making the first weekend of December a full weekend of holiday celebration.

There is a new reason to stroll downtown. Desert Paws Cat Café, Alamogordo's first cat café, celebrated its grand opening with a ribbon cutting on Wednesday, November 18, at 906 N. New York Ave.

Operated by the Abilities in Action Foundation and owned by Alamogordo native Tonia Finocchiaro, Desert Paws pairs a mission of providing work and education for people with disabilities or developmental delays with rescuing animals for adoption. Adoptable cats from local rescue Kitty City live in the café's cozy lounge, which guests can visit by reservation. Walk-in visitors can enjoy self-serve frozen yogurt with a toppings bar, coffee, cold brew, bubble tea and cat-themed gifts.

Cats adopted through Kitty City's standard application process stay at the café during review, and approved families pick up their new companion right at Desert Paws.

Hours: Wednesday–Friday 11 a.m.–8 p.m.; Saturday 10 a.m.–8 p.m.; Sunday noon–4 p.m.; closed Monday and Tuesday. Lounge reservations are booked through the Desert Paws Cat Cafe Facebook page.

Read the full story from 2nd Life Media: Desert Paws Cat Café Now Open in Alamogordo's Historic MainStreet District

Private investment continues to follow the public streetscape improvements on the 800 and 900 blocks. Three businesses are pressing ahead with rehabilitation and building modernization projects that will add dining, lodging and entertainment to the district.

Primo Bar and Restaurant and Bed and Breakfast – This project is rehabilitating and modernizing a historic downtown building to bring a bar, restaurant and bed-and-breakfast lodging to New York Avenue, giving visitors a place to eat, gather and stay in the heart of downtown. 

RAD Retrocade – Approved unanimously by the Alamogordo City Commission in 2025, owner Alex Macias's RAD Retrocade on the 800 Block is developing a retro arcade, bar and event venue, a family-friendly entertainment destination representing more than $1.2 million in private investment. 

Sands Theater – The historic Art Deco theater at 1017 New York Ave., which first opened as the White Sands Theatre in 1937, is undergoing a multimillion-dollar restoration. The project is a cornerstone of downtown's push toward a Cultural Arts District on the 1000 through 1200 blocks.

Alamogordo MainStreet is pleased to announce the appointment of Derrick Glover as Interim Executive Director.

Derrick recently retired as a U.S. Air Force Master Sergeant at Holloman Air Force Base and brings 24 years of military service, leadership and project management experience to the organization.

Already actively involved in preparations for Christmas on MainStreet, Derrick will work closely with the Board of Directors, downtown businesses and community volunteers to strengthen partnerships and continue revitalization efforts in historic downtown Alamogordo.

Alamogordo MainStreet also extends its appreciation to outgoing Executive Director Sven Sears for his service and wishes him well in his future endeavors.

The organization looks forward to this new chapter and encourages the community to welcome Derrick as he steps into his new role.

From a new café full of adoptable cats to historic buildings coming back to life, New York Avenue has more to offer than ever this holiday season. Shop small on November 28, celebrate the season on December 5, and stop in to say hello to Derrick and the businesses that make downtown special.

We look forward to seeing you on New York Avenue!
